ActivationGate.description:
When a policy is injected into an agent's prompt (Memory v2 #398).

Both gates are AND-combined with the policy's scope. Empty gate =
"no extra gating" (renders whenever the scope filter matches):

* ``tools`` — at least one tool here must be registered in the step.
* ``delegation`` — ``top`` = only the top-level (non-delegated)
  invocation; ``delegate`` = only sub-agent invocations; ``any`` = both.

``tags`` was a third gate and is gone (#932). It decided, invisibly,
whether a policy reached an agent: no screen ever showed it, and the gate
demanded EVERY listed tag while its own documentation promised any — so a
policy naming two roles reached nobody while the agent page displayed it as
applying. Linking the policy to the agent says the same thing in a table an
operator can see and edit.

The field is absent rather than deprecated-but-present: a row written
before #932 still carries the key, and ``extra="ignore"`` means reading one
drops it. Refusing it on READ would make an existing policy unloadable
instead of merely un-gated. Refusing it on WRITE is
:class:`ActivationGateRequest` below.
ActivationGate.title: ActivationGate

ActivationGateRequest.description:
The write side of :class:`ActivationGate` — refuses the retired gate.

Dropping ``tags`` from the model alone is not enough on a request: with
``extra="ignore"`` a caller would get HTTP 200 and a silently discarded
gate, which is the same invisible failure one level along. So a write that
still carries it is refused, and told what to do instead.
ActivationGateRequest.title: ActivationGateRequest

AddMemberRequest.description:
Give a colleague access to THIS workspace (#1100).

There is deliberately no tenant field, and unknown keys are rejected
rather than ignored: the workspace is always the caller's own
``auth.tenant_id``. A body that could name a tenant would re-create the
cross-tenant bypass PR #502 deleted, and silently dropping such a key
would let a caller believe it had been honoured.

AddMemberResponse.description:
The result of adding somebody, including the one-time password.

``temporary_password`` is present ONLY when the e-mail had no credential
yet and the platform therefore minted one. It is returned exactly once —
it is never stored in clear, never logged and never re-readable — and it
is ``None`` when the person already has an Axonity account, because they
keep the password they already use for their other workspace.

AdminLoginRequest.description:
The master key at ``/admin``: setup token + address + password.

Strict, like ``ClaimPlatformAdminRequest`` and for a related reason: this
is the one door a shut password policy does not close, so a body carrying a
key it does not declare is a 422 rather than something silently ignored.

All three fields are required and all three are checked. ``password`` has
the login minimum (1), not the signup minimum: this verifies a password
that already exists, and refusing a short one here would tell the caller
something about it.

email.description: The address of the platform administrator signing in. Nothing is created for it and nothing about it is changed.

token.description: The installation's SETUP_TOKEN, as set in its environment by whoever operates it. Bounded like a password so an oversized body is refused before any comparison is attempted.
token.title: Token

AdoptRepoRequest.description:
``POST /deployment/repos/adopt`` — PR the scaffold into an existing repo.

Names the repo by ``url`` OR ``fullName`` like the connect surface (#616
C3); the URL is parsed for shape only and the repo is then resolved against
the caller's VERIFIED installation bindings — a repo outside them is a 404,
whatever the request claims.

Unlike connect, the target is NOT required to be compliant: adoption is what
makes it compliant. A repo that already has an ``axonity.yaml`` has nothing
to adopt (422 — connect it instead). ``client`` defaults to the tenant slug.
AdoptRepoRequest.title: AdoptRepoRequest

AgentPermissions.description:
Capability flags + output guarding for an agent.

Booleans are the genuinely fixed capabilities (planning, delegation,
verbose output). Tool enablement (web search, code execution,
workspace files, etc.) lives on
``CreateAgentRequest.system_tool_ids`` so adding new tools doesn't
require a schema change.

Output guarding (issue #566) — the shapes the runtime already reads:

  * ``output_validators``       — passive submit_output gate
                                  (``tool_registry.py`` submit path)
  * ``exposed_validator_tools`` — pre-flight tools
                                  (``validator_tools.py``)
  * ``expected_output_schema_id`` — id-reference into the tenant
    schema library (= the library schema's ``name``). Authoring
    metadata at agent level; mandatory whenever validators are
    attached here.

``extra="allow"`` is load-bearing: production permissions carry
legacy keys (``code_execution``, ``output_via_slot_key_field``)
that an ``extra="ignore"`` round-trip would silently wipe on the
next UI save — the exact data-loss hazard this model closes.

Stored as JSONB on the agents table (snake_case keys via
``model_dump(exclude_none=True)`` in the routes).
AgentPermissions.title: AgentPermissions

AppRegisterRequest.description:
GitHub's App-Manifest redirect parameters, relayed by the FE.

``state`` is the signed token minted by ``GET/POST /app/register-url``; it —
not this request body — is what authorizes the registration. ``code`` is
the one-time manifest-conversion code GitHub issues on App creation.
AppRegisterRequest.title: AppRegisterRequest

AppRegisterResponse.description:
Confirms a completed registration — NEVER the private key or webhook
secret, which stay server-side (write-only from the client's perspective).
AppRegisterResponse.title: AppRegisterResponse

AppRegisterUrlRequest.description: Public instance origin and optional GitHub organization for setup.
AppRegisterUrlRequest.title: AppRegisterUrlRequest

AppRegisterUrlResponse.description:
The App-Manifest payload + target URL for self-registration.

The frontend auto-POSTs ``manifest`` to ``manifest_url`` (too large for a
GET link) so the operator sees GitHub's own confirmation page before
anything is created. ``manifest``'s keys are GitHub's OWN field names
(``default_events``, ``hook_attributes``, …) — a raw pass-through dict,
deliberately NOT camelCased like this API's other fields, because GitHub
requires them verbatim.
AppRegisterUrlResponse.title: AppRegisterUrlResponse

AppStatusResponse.description:
Whether THIS deployment has a GitHub App configured, and its public slug.

Read-only and secret-free (#671): gates the operator self-registration
surface — an UNCONFIGURED instance shows the register flow, a configured
one shows the App read-only with no register button. ``configured`` is
resolved DB-first, env-fallback (a SaaS env-var App reports ``true`` too),
so the register button never appears where an App already exists. ``slug``
is the App's PUBLIC GitHub slug (already exposed in install URLs), never a
credential — the private key, webhook secret and OAuth client secret stay
server-side and never cross this boundary. ``app_url`` uses APP_BASE_URL
when nonblank, then the saved public origin. ``app_url_editable`` is false
whenever APP_BASE_URL is set, even when that environment value is invalid.
AppStatusResponse.title: AppStatusResponse

One calendar on the date table: which column names which period.

a calendar is metadata on a table, not an entity of its own. A grain
left out is a grain this calendar does not have, and a window asking for
it is refused by name rather than answered from another grain.

grains.description: Grain → the column that names that period, for any of year, quarter, month, week, day.

ChangePasswordRequest.description:
Replace your own password, proving you know the current one (#1099).

The current password is re-asked even though the caller already holds a
valid session: a stolen access token is 15 minutes of read/write, and it
must not also be 15 minutes to take over the credential permanently.
ChangePasswordRequest.title: ChangePasswordRequest

ChannelReplyRequest.description:
An inbound reply from a non-chat channel (#777 S5, hardened by #986).

A channel adapter (email / WhatsApp webhook) POSTs the person's reply, the
reply secret it received in the outbound message, and **who the provider
says sent it**. There is no user session, so those two together are the
authorisation: the secret proves possession, the sender proves it came back
from the person we actually asked.

``sender`` is not optional and not advisory. Without it a forwarded reply
link is a complete credential, which is the property #986 removes.

sender.description: The channel identity the provider reports for the sender — an email address or phone number. Matched against the recipient the outbound message was addressed to; a mismatch is refused.
sender.title: Sender

token.description: The reply secret from the outbound message. NOT the run's wait token — that is a correlation id the platform stores in the clear.
token.title: Token

ChannelReplyRequest.title: ChannelReplyRequest

CiPlanRequest.description:
A plan request from the credentialed CI surface (``/deployment/ci/plan``).

Same body as :class:`ConfigPlanRequest` (a file-tree + optional source
provenance) plus an optional tenant GUARD. Like the ``ci/deploy`` credential
path, ``targetTenantId`` is a guard not a selector: when present it MUST equal
the deploy credential's single tenant, so a credential for environment A can
never plan environment B. The CLI omits it (the target is always the
credential's tenant); it exists so an explicit cross-tenant request is a clean
403 rather than a silent mis-target.
CiPlanRequest.title: CiPlanRequest

ClaimPlatformAdminRequest.description:
Give an existing account the administration of this installation.

**Strict on purpose, and this is the one field that matters.** The model
rejects any key it does not declare, so a body carrying ``password`` is a
422 rather than a silently ignored field — which is what keeps a reviewer,
and a future edit, from ever reading this as a door that could set one. The
setup token names who may DECIDE, never who somebody is.

email.description: The address of the EXISTING account that should administer this installation. Nothing is created for it.
email.title: Email

token.description: The installation's SETUP_TOKEN, as set in its environment by whoever operates it. Bounded like a password so an oversized body is refused before any comparison is attempted.
token.title: Token

ClaimPlatformAdminRequest.title: ClaimPlatformAdminRequest

CommitConfigRequest.description:
Request to commit the caller tenant's active config to a connected repo.

``full_name`` (``owner/name``) selects WHICH connected repo to commit to.
It is authorized server-side against the caller's VERIFIED installation
bindings (#549 F1) — a repo not on one of those installations resolves to a
404, whatever the request or a repo manifest claims. The length cap is a
DoS guard (a real ``owner/name`` is short).

``selection`` is optional: without it the whole workspace is committed, as
it always was.
CommitConfigRequest.title: CommitConfigRequest

CommitConfigResponse.description:
Result of a config commit — the pull request it opened.

``configured`` is False when the GitHub App is not set up (mirrors the
``/repos`` endpoint) so the UI can message it rather than treat a write
with no provider as an error. On success the PR fields are populated and
the FE surfaces the link. No credentials or provider tokens are included.
CommitConfigResponse.title: CommitConfigResponse

CommitPreviewRequest.description:
Ask what committing would CHANGE in the repository, without writing it.

``fullName`` names the repo the same way ``CommitConfigRequest`` does, and
is authorized the same way — against the caller's VERIFIED installation
bindings (#549 F1), never from the request's own claim.

``selection`` is optional, exactly as on the commit: without it this is the
preview of committing the WHOLE workspace, which is the commit an author
reaches for most and the one that used to have no preview at all.
CommitPreviewRequest.title: CommitPreviewRequest

CommitPreviewResponse.description:
What committing would change in the repository, and what cannot travel.

``files`` is the comparison against ``baseBranch`` — the pull request this
commit would open, before it is opened. ``carried`` / ``notCarried``
describe the SELECTION and are empty for a whole-workspace commit, which
has no selection to fall short of.
CommitPreviewResponse.title: CommitPreviewResponse

CommitSelectionSchema.description:
Which part of the workspace to commit, and how far to follow it.

``include_linked`` False commits exactly what was chosen — one edit, one
file. True commits everything the choice reaches: an agent's tools, its
delegates, their knowledge, and the processes the agent works in.

The list cap is a DoS guard AND a statement about what a selection is: a
human naming what they are committing. Committing everything has its own
call — omit the selection entirely.
CommitSelectionSchema.title: CommitSelectionSchema

CommitValuesResponse.description:
What the press wrote, and the grid as it now stands.

``commit_sha`` is ``None`` and ``files`` empty when nothing actually
changed — re-stating what the branch already says is a no-op, not an empty
commit that reads as "saved" and changed nothing.

The refreshed ``overview`` rides along so the screen never has to re-read to
see its own edit, and can never show a grid from before the commit.
CommitValuesResponse.title: CommitValuesResponse

ConcurrencyStatusResponse.description:
Live "X / Y concurrent runs" counter for the dashboard indicator.

``activeCount`` is non-archived runs in
``pending|running|waiting|input_required`` for this tenant; ``cap``
is the effective admin-set cap. The dashboard renders the ratio as
a progress strip so admins can tune before they hit the ceiling.

``runnableCount`` is how many of those are actually competing for the
ceiling: the same population minus every run that is waiting on live
work of its own (#1527). The two differ only under nesting, and that is
exactly when the single number misled — a fanned-out parent reports an
active status while it waits for children that have not started, so the
strip read cap/cap while children were still being admitted. Reading a
phantom saturation invites the one wrong reaction, raising the cap,
which moves the stall one level of breadth later.

Both numbers are reported rather than one being replaced: the alive
count is what everything else means by "running", and the second is what
says whether the ceiling is really full. Neither is the child-admission
gate's own number, which discounts the lineage of the specific child it
is admitting and is therefore per launch.

Effective per-tenant concurrent-active-run cap.

``isDefault`` is True when the tenant has no override and the response

* ``workflow_name`` — the list is tenant-wide, so a row has to say what
  it starts. An id does not.
* ``pending_tasks`` — how many of this trigger's ticks are waiting. It
  should be one. More than one means the schedule forked (#1278), and
  that shows up here as a number rather than as a workflow quietly
  running three times an interval.

One look at a condition, as a screen has to read it (#1354).

``met`` is the verdict and ``reason`` is why, in the words the evaluator
or the agent used — what an operator holds against the world. ``met`` is
``None`` while an agent is still judging, inside the run ``runId`` names.
``costMicros`` is what the look cost; an automatic look calls no model.

ConfigPlanRequest.description:
The plan request: EITHER a posted file-tree OR a connected-repo ref.

Supply exactly one source:

* ``files`` — a ``{path: content}`` tree (the same ``ConfigTree`` shape an
  import consumes), with optional ``source`` provenance. What CI / the app
  posts after serializing. Kept for back-compat.
* ``ref`` (+ ``refKind``) — a branch/tag of the tenant's CONNECTED repo the
  backend fetches (#549 F1) before diffing. What the Load & review UI (#553)
  sends; the repo is resolved from the persisted connection, never the body.

The target tenant is ALWAYS the caller's own (from the auth context), never
the request body.

ConfigPlanResponse.description:
A read-only dry-run diff of what a deploy would change.

``planId`` is the handle the frontend passes to publish so the commit applies
exactly what was previewed (see :func:`config_diff.compute_plan_id`).

``aftercare`` is the other half of the screen: what the deploy does NOT
settle (:mod:`src.services.config_aftercare`). It travels ON the plan rather
than on a second call of its own, because the judgement is about precisely
this version of this branch against this environment — a list fetched at
another moment than the button beside it is how a deploy reports success and
leaves the environment broken. A ``blocking`` line refuses the button.

Bounded by authorship, not by activity: one line per value the branch
declares as per-environment-required and one per trigger drawn on its
workflows. Nothing the platform does adds lines here.

``POST /deployment/connection`` — connect an environment link.

Persists a ``(full_name, branch, environment_name, auto_deploy)`` link
(#616 C1), naming the repo by ``url`` OR ``full_name`` (#616 C3). The repo is
authorized server-side against the caller's VERIFIED installation bindings
(#549 F1): a repo not on one of those installations is a 404, whatever the
request claims; ``branch`` must additionally exist AND carry a valid
``axonity.yaml`` on that ref (422 otherwise). ``branch`` and
``environment_name`` are required — the operator names WHICH branch = which
environment. ``auto_deploy`` is opt-in (default off) and never overrides the

subscribes to, and whether a verified push to that branch auto-deploys.

Request body configuration.

``form`` is ``application/x-www-form-urlencoded``: the shape the older
partner APIs speak, where the credentials are ordinary fields next to the
payload rather than a header. Its values are percent-encoded on
substitution — see ``_interpolate_form`` — so a ``&`` in a job title
cannot add a field the author never wrote.

``file`` sends a file of the run as the body (#1935): ``content`` names
the input carrying it (``{{document}}``) and ``max_bytes`` is the
receiver's limit. See ``domain/connector_file_body``.

Auto-pagination config — when enabled, the executor loops the request
until the page is incomplete or ``max_pages`` is reached.

Each iteration injects ``page_param`` and ``size_param`` into the input
parameters as numbers, so connector templates use ``{{page}}`` / ``{{size}}``
placeholders inside REST query params, GraphQL variables, or the body.

The connector returns the last page's raw response with the items at
``items_path`` replaced by the concatenated list of all pages' items.
Response mapping (JMESPath) is applied once to that aggregate.

returns its reference, ``{fileId, filename, contentType, sizeBytes}``.
``filename`` names it, and may use the inputs (``{{filename}}``). See
``domain/connector_file_response``.

ConnectorResponseTransform.description:
Optional server-side transform over the connector response.

A sandboxed function-tool ``implementation``
(``{imports, functions, classes, selectedPackages}``) executed in the
sandbox exactly like a function tool. Lets a connector slim a large
upstream payload to only the fields it needs, which JMESPath (no
recursive descent) cannot express.

The ``functions`` list MUST include one named ``run`` as the entry
point — ``run(input, response) -> dict`` — where ``input`` is the
resolved input params that drove the request and ``response`` is the
(post response-mapping) body.

schemaBody.description:
The JSON Schema document describing the output contract: `type`, `properties`, `required`, and — the part that is not JSON Schema — `validators`.

`validators` is a list of gates run against a submitted output. Each entry is one of two shapes.

A SHIPPED PREDICATE names `function` (e.g. `validators.min_length`), the `target` field it judges, and its own `args`. Omit `target` to judge the whole output.

A VALIDATOR TOOL names `tool` instead, and gets the STANDARD CALL — every authored validator is invoked the same way, so a screen can offer its inputs and a served spec can describe them:

  `data`    — what the validator is pointed at, untouched. The whole submitted output by default, or the field named by `field`.
  `slots`   — every declared session-memory reference found in `data`, with its text, indexed by the reference itself. The platform resolves these because sandboxed tool code is never handed a lookup callable.
  `binding` — what you declared, verbatim, so the validator knows which values in `data` are references rather than plain values.

Two keys steer it. `field` names the part of the output to hand over; leave it out for the whole output. `slots` lists the fields holding references, e.g. `["key", "source_key"]`. Both are checked on save: a `field` that is not a property, or a `slots` name the rows do not carry, is refused — a name that is not there would never be looked up and the gate would run on unresolved values in silence.

  {"tool": "my.freshness.check", "field": "units", "slots": ["key", "source_key"], "error_message": "REJECTED: {value}"}

A tool MAY instead declare `inputs` — the older, explicit binding, and the way a tool backed by a shipped predicate receives `value` plus its arguments. Each entry is `{"source": "field"|"const", "field": <name>, "as": "slot"?}`; with `as: "slot"` the field's value is read as a reference and the TEXT is passed. `field` may point into a list: `units[].key` is, from every row in `units`, the `key` field. A spec with `inputs` does not get the standard call.

`error_message` is the text an agent sees on refusal; `{value}` is replaced by what the validator reported.
schemaBody.title: Schemabody

DeployConfigRequest.description:
Deploy a config version to a target tenant.

Supply EXACTLY ONE source: ``files`` (a POSTed ``{path: content}`` file-tree
— what CI produces after checking out the repo, or the app after
serializing) OR ``source`` (a repo ref the backend fetches). ``targetTenantId``,
when set, is a guard, not a selector: it MUST equal the tenant the caller is
authorized for (the admin's own tenant, or the deploy credential's single
tenant) — a credential for env A can never deploy env B. ``configRef`` is an
optional human label for the posted-tree path (e.g. the CI commit sha); the
repo path derives it from the resolved commit.

``expectedPlanId`` (optional) pins the deploy to a previously previewed plan
(#548): the tree's content hash must match or the publish is rejected (409)
rather than silently applying drifted config. Honored on the admin ``/deploy``
path ("review → deploy"); the credentialed ``/ci/deploy`` path deliberately
does NOT pin (no interactive plan step) — see that route.

There is no approver field: a PROTECTED (production) environment is gated on
the caller being an interactive admin SESSION (#616 C2), which the request
body cannot assert.
DeployConfigRequest.title: DeployConfigRequest

DeployConfigResponse.description:
Outcome of a deploy — the import summary plus target + config version.

Per-type counts of entities ``created`` / ``updated`` / left ``unchanged``
(idempotent no-ops) / ``removed``, ``published`` (versioned entities taken
live via draft→publish), and the ``configRef`` that was deployed (the
resolved commit for a repo fetch). No credentials or tokens are ever
included.
DeployConfigResponse.title: DeployConfigResponse

DeployCredentialListResponse.description: The caller tenant's deploy credentials (metadata only, no tokens).
DeployCredentialListResponse.title: DeployCredentialListResponse

DeployCredentialResponse.description:
A deploy credential's metadata — NEVER its token.

Returned by list / revoke. The raw token exists only in the create/rotate
response (:class:`DeployCredentialWithTokenResponse`) and is unrecoverable
afterwards; only a hash is stored.
DeployCredentialResponse.title: DeployCredentialResponse

DeployCredentialWithTokenResponse.description:
A newly issued/rotated credential — carries the raw token ONCE.

``token`` is shown exactly once (at issue or rotate) and can never be
retrieved again; store it now. Every other endpoint omits it.
DeployCredentialWithTokenResponse.title: DeployCredentialWithTokenResponse

ExecuteConnectorRequest.description:
POST /api/v1/tools/execute-connector — request body.

Supports both REST and GraphQL connectors. GraphQL uses the
``query`` and ``variables`` fields; REST uses ``method``, ``path``,
``query_params``, and ``body``.
ExecuteConnectorRequest.title: ExecuteConnectorRequest

ExecuteStoredConnectorRequest.description:
POST /api/v1/tools/{tool_id}/execute-connector — request body.

Deliberately carries NOTHING but the call's inputs. The destination
(base URL, path, method, headers) and the credentials come from the
tenant's own connector row — that is the entire reason this route is
safe for a write-scoped service token where ``/tools/execute-connector``
is not. ``StrictCamelModel`` makes the contract enforceable: a body that
tries to smuggle a ``baseUrl`` or an ``authConfig`` is refused with a 422
rather than silently ignored, so an attempt to steer the request can
never look like it succeeded.
ExecuteStoredConnectorRequest.title: ExecuteStoredConnectorRequest

ExecuteStoredConnectorResponse.description:
POST /api/v1/tools/{tool_id}/execute-connector — response body.

Mirrors :class:`ExecuteConnectorResponse` minus ``responseHeaders``:
upstream headers routinely carry ``Set-Cookie`` and auth echoes, and a
test-run needs the body and the status, not the headers. Everything here
is already what the agent runtime hands a connector tool's caller.
ExecuteStoredConnectorResponse.title: ExecuteStoredConnectorResponse

ExecutorApplicationsResponse.description: The applications one executor may operate.

applicationIds.description: Ids of the live applications this executor may operate.
applicationIds.title: Applicationids

ExecutorApplicationsResponse.title: ExecutorApplicationsResponse

ExecutorCommandInfo.description: One command an executor knows (#1863 A4) — what a tool can ask for.
ExecutorCommandInfo.title: ExecutorCommandInfo

ExecutorResponse.description: An executor as the list and detail show it — never the secret.
ExecutorResponse.title: ExecutorResponse

ExecutorTokenResponse.description: Register — the ONLY place the plaintext token appears.
ExecutorTokenResponse.title: ExecutorTokenResponse

ExitToolSchema.description:
Structured contract for the tool that signals flow-step completion.

Stored as JSONB on flow_steps.exit_tool (required).
The ``json_schema`` is a JSON Schema object that validates the tool's
arguments at call time; forks may route on fields inside the payload.

Both fields are required so the runtime (``ToolRegistry._add_exit_tool``)
and the schema agree — passing ``{}`` is the explicit "no validation"
choice. A schema-side default would silently mask missing contracts.
ExitToolSchema.title: ExitToolSchema

ExpiringItem.description: A fact whose shelf life ends soon or ended (§12.3 *Expiring*).
ExpiringItem.title: ExpiringItem

ExposedValidatorTool.description:
One pre-flight tool exposure — wraps a registered validator as an
agent-facing tool (``validator_tools.py`` entry shape).

``error_message`` is allowed: production entries carry it as the
formatted failure template the wrapper returns on a failing check.
Snake_case on the wire for the same reason as :class:`ValidatorSpec`
— one declaration format at every level.

Like a submit-time spec, an exposure names EITHER a shipped predicate
(``validator_name``) or a validator tool from the library
(``validator_tool``), and each brings its own binding keys: the registry
form is bound by ``value_from_field`` + ``static_args``, the tool form by
``inputs``. Neither dispatch path reads the other's keys.

The reference key is ``validator_tool`` and not ``tool``, which is what a
submit-time spec calls it. An entry already carries ``tool_name`` — the
name the AGENT sees — and two keys a character apart meaning different
things is a trap that keeps costing. It pairs with ``validator_name``
instead: the two answers to what backs this exposure.
ExposedValidatorTool.title: ExposedValidatorTool

FactCard.description: Everything of §4.2 and §9.2 for one fact.
FactCard.title: FactCard

FactEventView.description: One entry of a fact's history (§5, §12): what happened, when, by whom, in which run.
FactEventView.title: FactEventView

FanOutProgress.description:
Per-state item counts for a fan-out — the shape the progress badge reads.

``total`` is the sum of all states (the "12 / 1500 done" denominator);
each per-state field is the count of ``task_queue`` rows in that state.

ONE shape for both scopes the UI asks about — a single batch on the run
page (:class:`BatchProgress`) and a whole launch on the runs list
(``RunSummary.for_each_progress``, epic #811 S1) — so the frontend
renders both through the same badge instead of growing a second one.
Tenant scoping is applied by the caller's repository query.
FanOutProgress.title: FanOutProgress

FanOutRateResponse.description:
The tenant-default fan-out pace (#817 S6).

``ratePerMinute`` is ``null`` when no default is set — the shipped
state, meaning fan-outs run as fast as the concurrency caps allow.
FanOutRateResponse.title: FanOutRateResponse

FillStatus.description:
What the last fill of this table did. Never part of a version.

A table that cannot say how old its rows are shows a failed overnight
fill as yesterday's truth — a confident figure with no reason to doubt
it.

lastError.description: Why the last fill wrote nothing, or null when it worked.
lastError.title: Lasterror

lastRowCount.description: How many rows the table held afterwards.
lastRowCount.title: Lastrowcount

nextAt.description: When the next fill is due. Null when it is paused.
nextAt.title: Nextat

FillStatus.title: FillStatus

FlowCloneRequest.description:
POST /api/v1/flows/{id}/clone — fork a visible flow.

``name`` is optional; the service defaults it to ``"<original> (copy)"``
so the UX can offer a one-click "Clone this flow" path.
FlowCloneRequest.title: FlowCloneRequest

FlowCreateRequest.description:
POST /api/v1/flows — create a new flow.

``flow_steps`` may be empty (a blank flow) or seeded with an initial
set. If provided, the caller can reference the entry point by name
via ``first_step_name``; the service resolves to the server-generated
step id.
FlowCreateRequest.title: FlowCreateRequest

FlowListItem.description: Lightweight flow row for the list view (GET /api/v1/flows).
FlowListItem.title: FlowListItem

FlowPromptStacksResponse.description: Resolved prompt stacks for every flow step of a single flow.

flowSteps.description: One entry per flow step in the flow.
flowSteps.title: Flowsteps

wildcardPrompts.description: Tenant wildcard snippets applied to the top of every flow step.
wildcardPrompts.title: Wildcardprompts

FlowPromptStacksResponse.title: FlowPromptStacksResponse

FlowSchema.description: Full flow detail returned by GET /api/v1/flows/{id}.
FlowSchema.title: FlowSchema

FlowStepPromptItem.description:
One per-step attachment of a snippet, with its target + order
inside that step. ``target`` and ``display_order`` belong to the
attachment — different steps can use the same snippet differently.
FlowStepPromptItem.title: FlowStepPromptItem

FlowStepPromptStack.description: A flow step and its resolved system/user prompt stacks.

flowId.description: Id of the flow this step belongs to.
flowId.title: Flowid

flowStepId.description: Flow step id — the placement target for attach/detach/reorder.
flowStepId.title: Flowstepid

flowStepName.description: Name of the flow step within its flow.
flowStepName.title: Flowstepname

stepId.description: Id of the owning workflow step; null when resolving a flow directly.

stepName.description: Name of the owning workflow step.
stepName.title: Stepname

stepType.description: Type of the owning workflow step (e.g. 'agent').
stepType.title: Steptype

systemPrompts.description: Snippets in the step's system stack, ordered by displayOrder.
systemPrompts.title: Systemprompts

userPrompts.description: Snippets in the step's user stack, ordered by displayOrder.
userPrompts.title: Userprompts

FlowStepPromptStack.title: FlowStepPromptStack

FlowStepSchema.description:
A flow-step as exposed in API responses and nested in create/update.

On create, ``id`` may be absent (server generates). ``transitions``
reference other steps by their ``name`` within the same flow when the
request lacks server-side IDs; the service layer resolves names to
UUIDs before persisting.

reasoningBudget.description: How many reasoning turns this step may take before it must wrap up. Leave empty for the platform default (50). A whole number between 1 and 500.
reasoningBudget.title: Reasoningbudget

variables.description: The variables the code that calls this method supplies, beyond the platform's standard ones. Leave empty for a step that needs none.
variables.title: Variables

wallClockBudget.description: How many seconds this step may spend reasoning before it must wrap up. Time spent waiting on delegates does not count. Leave empty for the platform default (3600). A whole number between 1 and 21600.
wallClockBudget.title: Wallclockbudget

FlowStepSchema.title: FlowStepSchema

FlowUpdateRequest.description:
PATCH /api/v1/flows/{id} — partial update with optimistic locking.

When ``flow_steps`` is provided it replaces the entire list (the
service diffs and preserves step IDs by matching on ``id`` then
``name``). Omitting the field leaves the steps untouched.
FlowUpdateRequest.title: FlowUpdateRequest

FollowBranchRequest.description:
Point THIS environment at ``branch``.

Only the branch: the environment's label, its flags and the chain branch it
belongs to are not the caller's to change here. A re-connect can change
those, and conflating the two is how a temporary experiment rewrites what
an environment IS.
FollowBranchRequest.title: FollowBranchRequest

FollowBranchResponse.description:
Where this environment points now, and where it goes home.

``homeBranch`` is on the answer because the screen needs it for the way
back, and because "is this environment on a detour?" is exactly
``branch != homeBranch`` — a question no screen should have to reconstruct
from a list somewhere else.
FollowBranchResponse.title: FollowBranchResponse

ForgetBlockerSchema.description: One reason the removal is refused, in one sentence.
ForgetBlockerSchema.title: ForgetBlockerSchema

ForgetEnvironmentEffectSchema.description:
What one environment sees, and when.

Every field of a row that is not ours comes from the manifest — a name and
a branch. What another workspace holds or deploys is never read, because
reading it is the cross-workspace read B8 exists to prevent.
ForgetEnvironmentEffectSchema.title: ForgetEnvironmentEffectSchema

ForgetPlanResponse.description: What taking this object out of the branch would do — before anybody says yes.
ForgetPlanResponse.title: ForgetPlanResponse

ForgetReferenceSchema.description:
One thing that still points at the object.

``detail`` is the author's own words for the place to look — the step
names, comma-separated — because "it is used" is nothing anybody can act on
and "Opstellen" is. Empty for a site with no finer place inside it.
ForgetReferenceSchema.title: ForgetReferenceSchema

ForgetResultResponse.description: The pull request that takes the object out of the branch.
ForgetResultResponse.title: ForgetResultResponse

ForgetTargetRequest.description:
The one object this request is about.

Strict: a misspelled key here would otherwise be silently ignored and the
request would act on whatever the remaining fields happened to name.
ForgetTargetRequest.title: ForgetTargetRequest

ForgotPasswordResponse.description:
The ONE answer this endpoint ever gives.

Identical for a known address, an unknown one, a suspended member and a
removed one — an endpoint that answers differently is a user-enumeration
oracle with a friendly label.
ForgotPasswordResponse.title: ForgotPasswordResponse

FormulaLeaf.description: One aggregation the formula will run, with the context that applies.

column.description: The column, or null for a row count.
column.title: Column

filters.description: The conditions pushed onto this part.
filters.title: Filters

ignores.description: The dimensions this part is deliberately free of.
ignores.title: Ignores

readFrom.description: Where this part came from, outermost first: every measure walked to reach it and then the table it reads, each with the version actually read. It is what makes a preview trustworthy — a chain read from drafts looks identical to the published one without it. Two parts that are the same work are ONE leaf, and then this names the first way to it.
readFrom.title: Readfrom

table.description: The table this part is aggregated over.
table.title: Table

via.description: The measures walked to get here, outermost first — what an explanation shows.
via.title: Via

window.description: The windows this part was read over, outermost first, each with its calendar by name: shift, to_date, rolling or running. Empty means it read the period the question asked for. A reader comparing two parts of one number has to be able to see that one of them is last year's.
window.title: Window

FormulaLeaf.title: FormulaLeaf

FormulaProblem.description: One refusal or warning: the code to repair on, the sentence to read.

code.description: The fixed code, as in formula-spec.
code.title: Code

message.description: What is wrong, in the author's words.
message.title: Message

severity.description: error blocks saving; warning does not.
severity.title: Severity

where.description: Where it sits: `offset` while the text is being read, `path` into the tree once there is one.
where.title: Where

FunctionEntry.description: A single function definition with its name and code.
FunctionEntry.title: FunctionEntry

GenerateInvoiceRequest.description: Make the statement of one ended month by hand (recovery, tests).
GenerateInvoiceRequest.title: GenerateInvoiceRequest

GetCompanyResponse.description:
GET /api/v1/company — full company with workflow summaries.

Document is None when the company was just auto-created (empty).
Frontend should show a "select template" prompt in this case.
GetCompanyResponse.title: GetCompanyResponse

effectiveSurfacing.description: What `surfacing` resolves to once the toolbox has had its say: 'always' (in every prompt) or 'on_demand' (found via discover_tools). Read this to answer 'is it in the prompt?'; read `surfacing` for the raw stored choice an edit form binds to.
effectiveSurfacing.title: Effectivesurfacing

environmentValues.description: Which of this tool's settings differ per environment, and how the deployment screen should present them (#1641 B15). Null when nobody has declared any.
environmentValues.title: Environmentvalues

publishedCredentialFields.description: Fields in the LIVE PUBLISHED snapshot that carry a literal credential, as markers naming where and what — e.g. "headers[0] 'Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key'" — never the value. Empty when the published version is clean or nothing is published. Non-empty means the running connector still sends a credential even if the fields above no longer do: cleaning a tool changes nothing until it is published (#1351).
publishedCredentialFields.title: Publishedcredentialfields

publishedMajorVersion.description: Major version currently live, or null when nothing is published. The runtime reads the published snapshot, not this record's fields — so this is what is actually running.
publishedMajorVersion.title: Publishedmajorversion

toolboxId.description: Id of the toolbox this tool belongs to, or null when it is in none. References a toolbox (GET /api/v1/toolboxes). A tool belongs to at most one.
toolboxId.title: Toolboxid

toolboxName.description: Display name of that toolbox, so a list can be grouped without a second lookup. Null when the tool is in none.
toolboxName.title: Toolboxname

GetWorkflowResponse.description:
GET /api/v1/workflows/{id} — full workflow with document.

``document`` contains the draft (working copy). The frontend uses this
for editing. ``draft_major_version`` and ``draft_version_name`` identify
which named version the draft represents (if any).

isPlatform.description: True when the platform ships this workflow (#1826): the editor opens it read-only, and it can be started but not changed.
isPlatform.title: Isplatform

GetWorkflowResponse.title: GetWorkflowResponse

GithubSetupRequest.description:
GitHub's post-install redirect parameters, relayed by the FE.

``state`` is the signed token minted by ``GET /install-url``; it — not
this request body — is what authorizes the binding. Length caps are
DoS guards: a real state is ~200 chars, an installation id a small int.
GithubSetupRequest.title: GithubSetupRequest

GithubSetupResponse.description: Acknowledges a verified installation → tenant binding.
GithubSetupResponse.title: GithubSetupResponse

GithubTokenConfigStatusResponse.description:
Whether a repo-scoped token is configured — never the token itself.

Deliberately carries NO token material: not the value, not a prefix, not a
length. ``configured`` is the only fact a client needs, and
``tenant_bound`` reports whether the stored credential is bound to the
CALLING tenant (a token bound elsewhere is unusable here — the connect
surface will list nothing, so the UI can say so instead of showing an
unexplained empty list).
GithubTokenConfigStatusResponse.title: GithubTokenConfigStatusResponse

GithubTokenConfigureRequest.description:
The operator's fine-grained, repo-scoped GitHub PAT.

Write-only: no response model ever echoes it back (see
:class:`GithubTokenConfigStatusResponse`). ``max_length`` bounds the body —
GitHub's fine-grained tokens (``github_pat_…``) are ~93 chars; 512 leaves
generous room for future formats without accepting an unbounded blob.
GithubTokenConfigureRequest.title: GithubTokenConfigureRequest

GrantSupportAccessRequest.description:
Enter a customer workspace, time-bounded and audited (#1109).

``reason`` is mandatory and has a minimum length because an optional
reason field is filled with "support" within a week. It is CUSTOMER-VISIBLE
— their admins read it in their own team list — so it is never a place for
internal detail.

``hours`` defaults to the configured default and is validated against the
configured ceiling server-side. A request above the ceiling is REFUSED,
not silently clamped: an operator who asked for a week should be told they
cannot have one, not handed a day and left believing otherwise.
GrantSupportAccessRequest.title: GrantSupportAccessRequest

GrantedAgent.description: An agent that was given this query's tool.
GrantedAgent.title: GrantedAgent

HiddenValueRequest.description: One value to take off this branch's screen, by its key.
HiddenValueRequest.title: HiddenValueRequest

ImportResult.description: Per-table count of rows written by an import.
ImportResult.title: ImportResult

InstallStubRequest.description:
POST /api/v1/_test/install-stub-provider — install a fresh
``ProviderRegistry`` containing a ``MockProvider`` keyed under
``stub`` and remap every model-router tier to that provider.

Caller queues a list of responses; the framework consumes them
in order over the run.
InstallStubRequest.title: InstallStubRequest

InstallUrlResponse.description:
The GitHub App install page URL for the "Connect GitHub" CTA.

``url`` carries the signed, single-use connect ``state`` (#549 F1) so
GitHub's post-install redirect can be tied back to the minting tenant.
``None`` when the App (or its public slug) is not configured — the UI
hides the install CTA instead of linking a bare, unverifiable install.
InstallUrlResponse.title: InstallUrlResponse

InvocationMessagesResponse.description:
One agent invocation's transcript, fetched on open (#875).

The body behind a row in ``RunDetail.agent_invocations``, which
carries metadata and a ``messageCount`` and no message bodies at all.
Same shape as :class:`RunValueResponse` and the session-memory file
read: the collection view carries handles, a body arrives when
someone asks to see it.

``messages`` is the FULLY DECODED conversation — a transcript stored
after #855 is marker-encoded on disk, and the repository resolves it,
so a caller never has to know which shape the row was written in.
Empty list for an invocation that has not taken a turn yet.
InvocationMessagesResponse.title: InvocationMessagesResponse

JudgementBody.description: Why a colleague rejects a fact — optional, kept with the event.
JudgementBody.title: JudgementBody

KnowledgeSettingsUpdate.description: A partial update: a field left out stays; ``null`` returns it to the start value.
KnowledgeSettingsUpdate.title: KnowledgeSettingsUpdate

KnowledgeSettingsValues.description: The rows of §15 as the workspace uses them (or the start values).
KnowledgeSettingsValues.title: KnowledgeSettingsValues

KnowledgeSettingsView.description: What the screen shows: the values, the start values, and which rows differ.
KnowledgeSettingsView.title: KnowledgeSettingsView

KnowledgeStep.description: One action of a learned instruction, by the element's label.
KnowledgeStep.title: KnowledgeStep

LandingPlace.description: One of the eight: a fact or a topic summary, with what hangs around it.
LandingPlace.title: LandingPlace

LayerSchema.description:
Layer within the company framework.

Layers are dynamic: users can add, remove, reorder, and hide them.
Each layer has a row/position for layout and per-view visibility flags.
LayerSchema.title: LayerSchema

LearningChoiceBody.description: The colleague's own judgement when the answer is not plainly the fact.
LearningChoiceBody.title: LearningChoiceBody

LearningItemView.description:
One question of a learning round, before it is answered: the question,
never the fact — that is shown once the colleague answered.
LearningItemView.title: LearningItemView

LearningMeasure.description: The measurement (§12.2): right answers on the random items, per workspace.
LearningMeasure.title: LearningMeasure

LearningReveal.description:
After the answer: the fact with its sources, percentage and passages, and
what the answer did. ``needs_choice``: say yourself whether you meant the same.
LearningReveal.title: LearningReveal

LearningRoundStatus.description: This month's round: how many items it holds.
LearningRoundStatus.title: LearningRoundStatus

LearningSchema.description:
The three learning fields of a workflow (#1923 AC1): whether the Spotter
runs, what it looks for, and whose answers are learned.
LearningSchema.title: LearningSchema

LearningTopicBody.description: The topic a colleague learns; ``null`` goes back to the one their role gives.
LearningTopicBody.title: LearningTopicBody

LessonView.description:
The reading before the questions of a topic (§12.2): the summaries of the
domain and the topic, as the graph holds them.
LessonView.title: LessonView

MajorVersionResponse.description: Response after creating a major version.
MajorVersionResponse.title: MajorVersionResponse

ManagedObjectRequest.description: One object to put on this branch's values list, by its group key.
ManagedObjectRequest.title: ManagedObjectRequest

MapNode.description:
One point or name on the map (§9.3): where it lies, which domain colours it,
and how certain it is (a fact's point is full when certain, pale as a draft).
MapNode.title: MapNode

MapWindow.description:
The nodes of one layer inside the visible plane, at most a bounded number:
``truncated`` says there were more — zoom in.
MapWindow.title: MapWindow

MarkActionVerdictRequest.description: A person's judgement of a verdict.

mark.description: right: the judge decided as it should. wrong: it should not have.
mark.title: Mark

note.description: Why, in a sentence, for the author.
note.title: Note

MarkActionVerdictRequest.title: MarkActionVerdictRequest

MeasureDefinitionPayload.description:
The calculation: how the number comes out of the rows.

**A measure is ONE expression** (#1908). ``expression`` is the whole of
it, as the formula text an author types or as the stored tree, and the
two are one-to-one. The fields below it — ``aggregation``, ``column``,
``numerator``, ``denominator`` — are the shape from before the formula,
kept while measures are migrated: one aggregation, or a division of two
parts, and nothing else.

aggregation.description: sum, average, count, count_distinct, min, max, latest (the value at the last date of each period — for a stock such as active customers) or ratio (numerator ÷ denominator). The shape from before the formula; write `expression` instead.
aggregation.title: Aggregation

column.description: The column it calculates over. Omitted for count and ratio.
column.title: Column

expression.description: The formula. Either the text an author types — `[net_revenue] - [variable_costs]`, `divide(sum(orders.cost), [orders_placed])` — or the stored tree. Both are accepted and they are one-to-one: the text parses to the tree and the tree writes back as the same text. GET /measures/formula-spec is the only valid list of words; never write one from memory.
expression.title: Expression

filters.description: Only rows meeting every condition count.
filters.title: Filters

quantity.description: What the number counts, in the words of the business: EUR, dogs, customers, orders, answers. Required for a single aggregation and derived for a formula. It is what lets the platform refuse adding euros to dogs — a 'number' format cannot, because it says how to show a figure and not what the figure is.
quantity.title: Quantity

target.description: The value the owner aims for.
target.title: Target

watchMargin.description: Within this many percent of the target on the wrong side reads 'watch'.
watchMargin.title: Watchmargin

MeasureDefinitionPayload.title: MeasureDefinitionPayload

MeasureDesignResponse.description:
A table's columns and time axis — what a number over it may ask for.

The MEASURES are no longer here (#1841). A measure belongs to the model,
not to one table, so "which measures are there" is a question about the
workspace and is answered by ``GET /api/v1/measures``. What a builder
still needs from a table is which columns it has and what dates its
rows carry.

calendars.description: The calendars on it, each naming the column that holds the year, the quarter, the month, the week and the day. What a window can be measured in.
calendars.title: Calendars

dateTable.description: Whether this is the workspace's date table.
dateTable.title: Datetable

MeasureDesignResponse.title: MeasureDesignResponse

dashboards.description: Every dashboard with a tile on this measure, by name. The other half of "used by": a measure that twelve numbers rest on and four screens show is not a measure anybody changes lightly.
dashboards.title: Dashboards

dependsOn.description: Every measure this one rests on, by name — the WHOLE chain, not only what its formula names. Publishing reads it: certified is the whole chain, not only the top of it.
dependsOn.title: Dependson

formula.description: The formula as TEXT, with names — the one spelling, written by the server from the stored tree. The tree is in `definition` and names things by id, which is what makes a rename break nothing; this is what a person reads and types. Empty for a measure that carries no formula.
formula.title: Formula

readsTables.description: Every table this measure reads, by name. Two of them for a measure that compares two fact tables.
readsTables.title: Readstables

tableName.description: The home table's name, or null for a measure comparing two.
tableName.title: Tablename

usedBy.description: Every measure that rests on this one, by name. What a refusal lists when somebody deletes a basis, and what a screen shows before they change one — twelve numbers may move with it.
usedBy.title: Usedby

MeasureFilterPayload.description: One condition a row must meet to count.

operator.description: equals, not_equals, in, not_in, greater_than, less_than, at_least or at_most. The last four need a number or date column.
operator.title: Operator

value.description: What the column is compared with; a list for in and not_in.
value.title: Value

MeasureFilterPayload.title: MeasureFilterPayload

unit.description: number, currency or percent (a percent is stored as a fraction: 0.49 is 49%).
unit.title: Unit

MeasurePartPayload.description: One side of a ratio: a sum, a count, or a count of distinct values.

column.description: The column it reads. Omitted for count, which counts rows.
column.title: Column

filters.description: Conditions on THIS side's rows. Where the two sides read different tables this is the only place a filter can go: a filter on the measure itself names a column only one of the two tables has.
filters.title: Filters

table.description: The table THIS side reads, when it is not the measure's own. Give it on both sides to compare two fact tables — they are not joined: each side is aggregated over its own rows and the two results are divided per period and per group.
table.title: Table

MeasurePartPayload.title: MeasurePartPayload

MeasureQueryItem.description: One tile's question: a measure, over a period, maybe split.

compare.description: What the total is compared with.
compare.title: Compare

end.description: Last day of a custom range, inclusive.
end.title: End

explain.description: Also hand back the value of every PART of the formula — on the total, on each point of the series and on each group. "The margin fell" is not an explanation; "revenue held and cost rose" is. Off by default: a tile wants a number.
explain.title: Explain

filters.description: Extra conditions, on top of the measure's own.
filters.title: Filters

grain.description: Draw a series per this grain; auto picks one that fits; none draws no series.
grain.title: Grain

key.description: The caller's own id for this question; the answer carries it back.
key.title: Key

limit.description: With a split: how many groups, largest first.
limit.title: Limit

measure.description: The measure's name — the handle it carries in the model, unique in this workspace.
measure.title: Measure

period.description: A named period. Omit (null) and send start and end for a custom range.
period.title: Period

splitBy.description: A column to split the measure by.
splitBy.title: Splitby

start.description: First day of a custom range.
start.title: Start

tableId.description: The table the tile was authored against. Optional, and no longer what finds the measure: a measure belongs to the model and is named (#1841). A measure that compares two fact tables has no single table at all.
tableId.title: Tableid

useDraft.description: Read the working definition instead of the published one — for an author previewing a measure before publishing it. The measures it CALLS still resolve to their published definitions; ask for useDraftChain as well to read their drafts too.
useDraft.title: Usedraft

useDraftChain.description: Also read the working definitions of the measures UNDER this one. A different question from useDraft: certified means the whole chain, so a preview of a margin must not silently recompute every basis beneath it from unpublished work. The answer says per part which version each thing behind it was read from.

OAuthAuthorizeUrlResponse.description:
``GET /deployment/github/oauth/authorize-url`` — the "Connect GitHub" CTA.

``url`` is GitHub's authorize page carrying a signed, single-use,
tenant+user-bound ``state`` (#630) so the callback can't be forged or
cross-bound. ``None`` when the App's OAuth client is not configured (DB or
env) — the UI hides the CTA instead of linking an unusable page.
OAuthAuthorizeUrlResponse.title: OAuthAuthorizeUrlResponse

OAuthCallbackRequest.description:
GitHub's post-authorize redirect parameters, relayed by the FE (#630).

``state`` is the signed token minted by ``/authorize-url``; it — not this
body — is what authorizes and binds the connection. Length caps are DoS
guards: a real ``code`` is short, a state ~200 chars.
OAuthCallbackRequest.title: OAuthCallbackRequest

OAuthCallbackResponse.description: Acknowledges a connected GitHub identity — NEVER any token material.
OAuthCallbackResponse.title: OAuthCallbackResponse

OAuthConnectRequest.description:
``POST /deployment/github/oauth/connect`` — bind-then-connect (#630 1b).

Under Option 1 OAuth access IS the authority: the admin picks a repo from
their visible list (which carries the ``installationId``) and this establishes
the tenant's installation binding from that authority, then links the repo.

``installationId`` is NOT trusted as sent — the service re-verifies it against
the calling admin's OWN GitHub user token before binding (a client could POST
any id). ``fullName`` names the repo directly (no URL parsing — it came from a
resolved candidate). ``branch`` / ``environmentName`` are the environment link
(#616 C1); ``autoDeploy`` opt-in (never overrides the protection gate);
``protected`` is additive (#616 C2). Length/range caps are DoS guards.
OAuthConnectRequest.title: OAuthConnectRequest

OAuthScaffoldConnectRequest.description:
``POST /deployment/github/oauth/scaffold-and-connect`` — make a NON-compliant
repo compliant, then connect it (#630 Phase 2a).

For a repo the admin can see but which has no valid ``axonity.yaml``: Axonity
DIRECT-COMMITS the scaffold to a FRESH branch (never a PR, never the default
branch) and links the repo on that branch. ``installationId`` is re-verified
against the admin's OWN GitHub token before anything is written (a client id
is never trusted). ``branch`` optionally overrides the fresh branch name
(default ``axonity-config``); ``environmentName`` is the environment link.
An already-compliant repo skips the scaffold and just connects. Length/range
caps are DoS guards.
OAuthScaffoldConnectRequest.title: OAuthScaffoldConnectRequest

OAuthStatusResponse.description:
``GET /deployment/github/oauth/status`` — booleans only, never a token.

``configured`` is whether the App's OAuth client is set up on this instance;
``connected`` is whether the CALLING admin has linked their own GitHub
identity. Deliberately carries no token material of any kind (#630 AC6).
OAuthStatusResponse.title: OAuthStatusResponse

QueueDispatchHealth.description:
Dispatch liveness — "is anything actually moving?".

``run_queue_depth`` is process-local (see module docstring). It is
paired with the last observed worker heartbeat so the screen can say
"work is queued but not being processed" instead of showing a
silently growing pending count.

**Two shapes, by role — this is a tenant-isolation boundary.** The
three numeric fields describe the backend PROCESS, not the caller's
tenant: polled every few seconds by any authenticated member they
compose into a platform-wide load-and-throughput timeseries that
includes every other tenant's activity. So:

  * **administrator** — the full block: ``run_queue_depth``,
    ``last_tick_at``, ``seconds_since_tick``, ``healthy``,
    ``unhealthy_reason``.
  * **member (anything that is not ``role == "admin"``)** — the three
    numeric fields are ``None``; ``healthy`` and ``unhealthy_reason``
    are unchanged.

``healthy`` / ``unhealthy_reason`` are never degraded: they are the
operational signal ("dispatch is down") a member needs to stop
waiting on a run, and they carry no volume information. The split is
applied in ``QueueOverviewService.overview``; the frontend mirror
(``frontend/src/lib/workflow/types/queues.ts``) must type the three
numeric fields as nullable for every caller.
QueueDispatchHealth.title: QueueDispatchHealth

QueueOverview.description: Single payload behind the health tiles.
QueueOverview.title: QueueOverview

QueueRunRow.description:
One row in the "In flight" pane — a run that has not finished.

``current_step_name`` / ``wait_reason`` are derived server-side from
the run's ``step_states`` so an operator can tell "waiting for an
answer since 3h" apart from "running step 4 of 9" without opening
the run.
QueueRunRow.title: QueueRunRow

QueueTaskCounts.description:
Per-state counts of active task-queue rows.

Mirrors ``schemas.task_queue.DashboardSummary`` plus a ``total`` so
the tiles can show throughput, not only problems. Dismissed rows are
excluded — the operator cares about the active backlog.
QueueTaskCounts.title: QueueTaskCounts

A doc reaches an agent through an explicit ``agent_reference_docs``

tenant-wide. The composed list used to mix them with no discriminator,
so "detach this document" looked like a sensible request for a doc that
was never linked — and the detach answered "done". Explicit link wins;
see ``services/link_source.py``.

Answer to attaching / detaching a reference doc (#778).

``detached`` / ``attached`` say what ACTUALLY happened, not what was
asked for. ``still_in_scope`` is the other half of the truth: removing
a link does not switch off a doc that is also tenant-wide, and
``link_source`` then names why it stays.

ReleaseApprovalItem.title: ReleaseApprovalItem

ReleaseApprovalSummary.description:
One row of the release queue — the counts, never the closure.

Deliberately WITHOUT ``members``. A release's closure grows with what the
tenant has authored (Talentus: 162 entities), so embedding it once per row
would make the queue's response grow with the tenant — the nested
unbounded collection B-NB8 exists to keep off the wire. The members are
what the approver reads to decide, and deciding happens on one release:
``GET /publish-approvals/release/{id}`` carries them.

The verdict here is the one RECORDED when the release was requested, and
``readiness_as_of`` says when that was. Recomputing it would mean walking
a full closure per row on every poll of the queue. The two moments that
must be true now — showing the decision and taking it — are the detail
route and ``approve``, both of which recompute (#793).
ReleaseApprovalSummary.title: ReleaseApprovalSummary

Aggregate outcome of ``release_bulk``.

``released`` of ``total``. Rows that had already started, finished or
carried no moment are simply not counted — see ``release_bulk`` for

Outcome of ``release_now``.

``status='released'`` — the row's moment moved to now and the next
claim will pick it up. ``status='no_change'`` — the row carried no
moment and was already free to be claimed, which is an answer rather
than an error.
ReleaseResult.title: ReleaseResult

Correct a workspace's display name.

Only the name. The slug is deliberately not accepted: it lives in URLs
people have bookmarked and in anything built against this workspace, so
changing it is a migration rather than a correction. Strict, so a body that
tries is a 422 rather than a field quietly dropped.

ReorderSnippetsRequest.title: ReorderSnippetsRequest

ReplayBulkBody.description:
Request body for ``POST /task-queue/replay-bulk``.

Either ``ids`` (an explicit list, max 500) or ``filter`` (apply the
same predicate the inspector uses) — exactly one. The route layer
rejects "both" and "neither" with HTTP 422.
ReplayBulkBody.title: ReplayBulkBody

ReplayBulkResult.description:
Aggregate outcome of ``replay_bulk``.

Counts the three legitimate outcomes per the issue's acceptance:

  * ``succeeded`` — rows transitioned to pending in this call.
  * ``conflicted`` — rows that were already pending (idempotent
    no-ops; not an error).
  * ``errored`` — rows that could not be replayed (cross-tenant /
    not found / unexpected failure). Errors are sanitised; the
    per-row reason lives in the audit log.
ReplayBulkResult.title: ReplayBulkResult

ReplayResult.description:
Outcome of ``replay_one``.

``status='replayed'`` — row was non-pending and is now pending.
``status='no_change'`` — row was already pending; replay is a no-op
(TASK-QUEUE-DESIGN.md §9.3: replay is idempotent).
ReplayResult.title: ReplayResult

RepoBranchesResponse.description:
``GET /deployment/repo-branches`` — a connected-repo's real branches.

The validated branch list the connect UI's branch picker (#616 C1 / #619)
offers instead of a free-text field. Scoped to the caller's VERIFIED
installation binding (#549 F1): a repo the tenant has no binding for is a
404, never a provider-wide enumeration.
RepoBranchesResponse.title: RepoBranchesResponse

RepoSelector.description:
A repo named by URL OR ``owner/name`` — exactly one (#616 C3).

The URL is INTENT, not authority: it is parsed to ``owner/name`` and then
RESOLVED only through the caller's verified binding, so a pasted URL widens
access to nothing. Exactly one of ``url`` / ``full_name`` must be supplied.
``url`` accepts ``https``/``.git``/``git@…``/``/tree/<branch>`` forms; a
malformed or foreign URL is a 422 with no provider call for a foreign repo.
RepoSelector.title: RepoSelector

RepoSummary.description:
A repository on the caller's verified installations + its state.

Scoping is the server-verified installation binding (#549 F1). Every repo
listed here sits on one of the caller's OWN bindings — the list reports
non-compliant repos (#616 C3), but only ever ones the tenant demonstrably
controls, so ``reason`` never describes a repo outside those bindings.

``compliant`` = the Axonity App is installed AND a valid ``axonity.yaml``
exists. When False, ``reason`` says which half is missing and the UI shows
the repo greyed with a fix-it affordance instead of silently dropping it —
the silent-empty-list bug this story exists to kill. ``client`` / ``tenant``
/ ``environments`` come from the manifest, so they are null/empty exactly
when ``compliant`` is False.

``manifest_tenant_matches`` is a consistency flag only — False means the
repo's own manifest declares a different tenant slug and the UI should show
a warning, not that the repo is unauthorized. No credentials or provider
tokens are ever included.
RepoSummary.title: RepoSummary

ResetLinkResponse.description:
A password-reset link an admin hands over themselves (#1132).

``path`` is RELATIVE — ``/reset-password?token=…`` — and the client
prefixes its own origin. The admin is looking at the application in their
browser, so that origin is already the right one and cannot be wrong, and
nothing has to be configured for the link to work. Which matters: the
platform cannot send mail yet, and this exists precisely because of that.

Readable exactly once, like the temporary password beside it. The token is
stored only as a digest, so nothing can produce it again.
ResetLinkResponse.title: ResetLinkResponse

ResetPasswordRequest.description: Redeem a reset link and set a new password (#1105).
ResetPasswordRequest.title: ResetPasswordRequest

ResolveConnectableResponse.description:
``POST /deployment/resolve-connectable`` — is this repo connectable?

Fail-closed (#616 C3): a repo the tenant has no verified binding for (or one
without a valid manifest) resolves to ``connectable: false`` with a
human-readable ``reason`` — never silently dropped. When connectable, the
repo's real ``branches`` + ``default_branch`` are returned so the connect UI
can populate its branch picker in one round-trip; ``branch_hint`` echoes a
branch parsed from a ``/tree/<branch>`` URL so the UI can pre-select it.

**``reason_code`` is not an oracle, and the split matters.** It takes two
kinds of value:

* ``no_manifest`` / ``invalid_manifest`` — only ever for a repo INSIDE the
  caller's verified bindings. Safe to be specific: the tenant demonstrably
  controls that repo (Gate 1 — only a GitHub admin of it could install the
  App), so this tells them nothing they cannot already see, and it is what
  lets the UI offer "add a manifest" instead of a dead end.
* ``app_not_installed`` — for anything else. It describes the CALLER's
  OWN binding state ("no binding of yours covers that"), not the repo, and
  is returned identically for a repo that does not exist, one that is
  private to another org, and one that exists but is unbound. That
  indistinguishability is deliberate: pasting a victim's URL must never
  reveal whether it exists. ``reason`` stays generic in this case too.
ResolveConnectableResponse.title: ResolveConnectableResponse

RestartAcknowledgement.description:
A restart was asked for and recorded; the process stops in a moment.

The delay is what lets this answer arrive at all: the process that serves
the request is the one being stopped, so it replies first and stops after.

inSeconds.description: How long until this process stops. The API is unreachable while the container comes back.
inSeconds.title: Inseconds

RestartAcknowledgement.title: RestartAcknowledgement

Response after un-deleting an entity.

``restored`` is ``False`` when the entity was already live — the
operation is idempotent, so that is a success, not an error, and the
flag lets a caller tell "I brought it back" from "it was never gone".
RestoreEntityResponse.title: RestoreEntityResponse

RestoreResponse.description: Response after restoring from a version snapshot.
RestoreResponse.title: RestoreResponse

RevealSecretResponse.description:
POST /api/v1/secrets/{id}/reveal — the decrypted credential.

The ONE response in this module that carries a value. It exists because an
administrator moving an installation to another environment has to type the
same credentials in again, and the platform is holding them.

``id`` and ``name`` travel with the value so a screen showing several
secrets cannot put a value on the wrong row.

``value`` is the whole credential, not one field of it: an OAuth2
credential is a client id AND a client secret, and returning half of it
sends somebody back to the vendor for the other half.
RevealSecretResponse.title: RevealSecretResponse

RevealedWebhookAddress.description:
``POST /webhook-triggers/{id}/reveal`` — the full address, once.

``id`` and ``name`` travel with it for the same reason the secrets reveal
carries them: a screen showing several webhooks must not be able to put an
address on the wrong row.
RevealedWebhookAddress.title: RevealedWebhookAddress

RhythmPayload.description:
WHEN a table fills, and how the rows are written — #2013.

What used to be one bag with the SQL in it. The SQL, the source and
the grain left for the query that fills the table; what stays here is
the part that belongs to the TABLE, because a query returns rows and
something else fires it.

Sending no rhythm at all is a choice: then nothing starts by itself
and **Refresh now** is the only thing that fills the table.

cron.description: When it fills, as a cron expression in its timezone. Empty means it never fills by itself — only when someone asks.
cron.title: Cron

enabled.description: False pauses it: the table keeps every row it has and gets no next turn. Different from having no rhythm, which says the author never wanted one.
enabled.title: Enabled

keyColumns.description: Which columns identify a row, for an upsert — usually the date plus whatever the query splits by. An append writes a key nowhere, so naming one there is refused.
keyColumns.title: Keycolumns

mode.description: `upsert` replaces the rows that match the key and adds the rest, so a re-run of the same day does not double it. `append` adds what came back.
mode.title: Mode

timezone.description: The zone the cron expression is read in.
timezone.title: Timezone

RhythmPayload.title: RhythmPayload

RightVersionBody.description: The right version of a fact that was corrected as wrong without one.
RightVersionBody.title: RightVersionBody
