RollbackTargetResponse.description: What "Terug naar vorige versie" would do, before you press it (B9).
RollbackTargetResponse.title: RollbackTargetResponse

RouteKindOption.description: One way of reaching a model, and whether this build can do it.

isExecutable.description: False means storable but not callable — the shape is ready and no client speaks it, so the screen must not offer it as if a model would run.
isExecutable.title: Isexecutable

RouteKindOption.title: RouteKindOption

RuleCount.description: How one rule fared: how often it said no, how often that was wrong.

rule.description: The rule the judge named; empty when it named none.
rule.title: Rule

RuleCount.title: RuleCount

RunCaller.description:
The process that called this one, when another process did (#1375).

A sub-process invocation appears on the called workflow's own runs
list, where it would otherwise be indistinguishable from a run someone
started by hand. That difference matters to an operator deciding
whether to re-run it: you do not re-run a step of somebody else's
process, you re-run that process.

``run_id`` is the caller's run, so the row can link back to it — the
invocation's real context is inside there.
RunCaller.title: RunCaller

RunCostBreakdownEntry.description:
One row of per-agent + per-model cost rollup (S205.3, V7 §9.3).

``tokens_in`` is the TOTAL prompt tokens; ``cached_tokens`` is the
cache-served subset of it. ``input_cost_micros`` prices only the
uncached remainder; ``cached_cost_micros`` the cached subset at its own
rate — so the total = input + cached + output, exactly.

Those three are what the calls in this group were BILLED at, read from
the ledger. ``None`` means these rows predate the split being recorded:
the total stands, the breakdown of it is not recoverable, and a zero
would say something untrue about it.
RunCostBreakdownEntry.title: RunCostBreakdownEntry

RunCostResponse.description:
Aggregate cost surface for a single run (S205.3, V7 §9.3).

For active runs: aggregated fresh from ``run_cost_entries`` on every
request.  For terminal runs (completed / failed / cancelled): the
breakdown is the JSONB snapshot written at finalization.

Cost is in micro-units of ``currency`` — clients format to display.

currency.description: What the micros ARE. A run totals one currency: runs from before the euro prices say USD, and the ledger refuses to fold a differently-denominated amount into an existing total.
currency.title: Currency

RunCostResponse.title: RunCostResponse

RunDetail.description: Full run detail with step states.
RunDetail.title: RunDetail

RunInputFileResponse.description:
A file a run will start with (#1824): the reference, never the bytes.

This is exactly what the start form puts into ``triggerInput`` for a file
parameter — the run carries the reference, the bytes stay in storage for
as long as the run lives.
RunInputFileResponse.title: RunInputFileResponse

RunItemResult.description:
One row inside a launch: what happened to one item (epic #811 S3).

A deliberately THIN projection of a child run. The list it feeds can be
thousands of rows long, so it carries what an operator scans for —
which person, what happened, when — and nothing else. Anything deeper
lives one click away, on that item's own run detail at ``id``.

``status`` is the child run's own status and drives the status badge.
``skipped`` is the fact the status cannot carry: a gate deliberately
declined this item (``SKIP <category>: <reason>``), which the run
correctly records as a clean success. Without the flag every
deliberately skipped person would read as processed. ``skip_reason``
is the parsed BUSINESS reason only — never the raw exception text.
RunItemResult.title: RunItemResult

RunOutlineCounts.description:
How a node's children came out, without listing them.

A fan-out step's roll-up. ``truncated`` is how many items the outline
deliberately did not list — the operator is never left to infer that
forty was all of them.
RunOutlineCounts.title: RunOutlineCounts

RunOutlineItemsResponse.description:
Response from ``GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/outline/items``.

The next stretch of ONE fan-out step's items, as outline nodes — the
item and the steps beneath it, exactly as the outline itself sends
them, so a spliced-in stretch is indistinguishable from the first.

``next_offset`` is ``None`` on the last stretch. A client that reads it
never has to ask again to find out there is nothing left.
RunOutlineItemsResponse.title: RunOutlineItemsResponse

RunOutlineNode.description:
One node in a run's outline (#941).

The outline is the run's table of contents: everything that happened,
nested at the depth it happened. Steps, the items a fan-out handed out,
and — from #942 — the delegates and plan activities beneath them.

Deliberately carries NO bodies. Its size is a function of the run's
SHAPE rather than its content, which is what lets one realtime tick
refetch it for a launch over four thousand items at the same cost as
for one over four. Bodies are fetched per node, when a node is opened.

Flat, with parent pointers — the client nests it. A flat list is
trivially cacheable, diffable and pageable; a nested response is none
of those.
RunOutlineNode.title: RunOutlineNode

RunOutlineResponse.description:
Response from ``GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/outline`` (#941).

``item_cap`` is the number of items listed per fan-out step; anything
beyond it is counted in that step's ``counts.truncated`` and lives on
the paged item-results surface.
RunOutlineResponse.title: RunOutlineResponse

RunQueryResult.description:
What a query answered, and what it cost.

``rows`` is bounded by the service's ceiling, so this object cannot grow
with the warehouse. ``truncated`` says when rows were left unread — a
number shown as complete when it is not is the outcome this surface may
never produce.
RunQueryResult.title: RunQueryResult

RunQueryTestRequest.description: Run this query once, with these values, and show what came back.

maxRows.description: How many rows to show. Clamped to the platform's ceiling.
maxRows.title: Maxrows

values.description: A value per declared parameter. They are BOUND, never written into the statement.
values.title: Values

RunQueryTestRequest.title: RunQueryTestRequest

RunRestartResult.description:
Outcome of re-dispatching a stuck run.

``status='restarted'`` — the run was re-queued onto the RunQueue.
``status='already_active'`` — it was already being processed, so the
call was an idempotent no-op (double-click safe).
RunRestartResult.title: RunRestartResult

RunStopBulkBody.description:
Body of the bulk-stop call — explicit ids only, never a filter.

Capped so one request cannot cancel an unbounded number of runs; the
UI's selection model tops out at one page anyway.
RunStopBulkBody.title: RunStopBulkBody

RunStopBulkResult.description: Per-outcome tally of a bulk stop.
RunStopBulkResult.title: RunStopBulkResult

RunStorageResponse.description:
What this tenant's run history costs, split by retention class.

Backs the operator view behind ``GET /api/v1/runs/storage`` (#863 S2).
The split is the point: retention keeps CONVERSATIONS forever and
expires the OPERATIONAL payload, so a single total tells an operator
nothing about what a horizon would actually reclaim.

Bytes are as-stored (post-compression), i.e. what a sweep would give
back — not uncompressed payload, and not the table size, which
includes indexes and per-row overhead this cannot attribute to a
tenant.
RunStorageResponse.title: RunStorageResponse

RunTaskItem.description:
One row in the run-detail Tasks panel (#382 CP5).

Two shapes share this schema:

* ``type="task"`` — a row from ``task_queue`` whose ``parent_run_id``
  is this run (FOR EACH iteration not yet promoted, ``delegate_task``,
  callback wake-task, compensation, …). ``status`` carries the
  task_queue state (``pending``/``in_progress``/``succeeded``/…).
* ``type="run"`` — a *child Run* spawned by this run (today only
  FOR EACH iterations land here, identified via
  ``triggered_by_type='for_each'`` + ``trigger_payload.parent_run_id``).
  ``status`` carries the run status; ``promoted_run_id`` is set so
  the frontend can route a click to ``/digitaltwin/runs/<id>``.

The frontend renders both kinds in a single list so the operator
sees the full lineage from this run's perspective.
RunTaskItem.title: RunTaskItem

RunTraceEntry.description:
One tool call in the run's chronological trace.

Sourced from the automation plan-step records that
``automation_executor`` already writes onto each step's state — both
on the parent run and on any iteration child runs spawned by a
for-each / iteration step. This is purely a derived view; the
underlying data is the ``plan_step_records`` JSONB column already
being persisted today.
RunTraceEntry.title: RunTraceEntry

RunTraceResponse.description:
Full chronological trace of tool calls across the run + its
iteration children.
RunTraceResponse.title: RunTraceResponse

RunValueMarkerSchema.description:
The stand-in a large value leaves behind in ``step_states`` (#839).

``GET /runs/{run_id}`` serves ``step_states`` as STORED. Every subtree
at or above the run-value threshold was replaced by this three-key
marker on write (``src/repositories/run_values.py``), so a list
mentioned in three places crosses the wire ONCE — as three identical
~90-byte markers — instead of three times in full. Whoever opens it
fetches the body from ``GET /runs/{run_id}/values/{digest}``.

Two deliberate choices:

* **Explicit ``$``-prefixed aliases, not camelCase.** The realtime hub
  publishes the JSONB column verbatim, so the marker reaches the client
  that way regardless; matching it here means ONE client-side reader
  handles the REST response and the realtime row.
* **``extra="forbid"``**, mirroring ``run_values.is_marker``. Tenant
  data may legitimately carry a ``$run_value`` field of its own, and a
  loose model would swallow the rest of that object's keys.

RunValueResponse.description:
One stored run value, fetched when someone opens it (#839 S2).

``value`` is the value as STORED, so a value that wraps another large
value carries its marker in turn — the client resolves one level at a
time rather than pulling a whole tree it may not display. Size and
shape are not repeated here: the marker the caller already holds
carries both.

RunWaitingOnResponse.description:
Payload of ``GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/waiting-on``.

Empty ``items`` is a valid state — a run in ``waiting`` may have
every wake-task already terminal (about to resume), or simply not
have any wake-tasks attached yet. The frontend renders the panel
only when ``items`` is non-empty.

RuntimeTopologyResponse.description:
What this installation is actually running, and what it will run next.

Everything here is a stored SETTING — the topology and the five pool
numbers alike — and every one of them takes effect when the container
restarts, because the supervisor reads them once at boot and a running
process never changes shape. ``runningExecutionMode``, ``restartRequired``
and each pool's ``runningCeiling`` exist for exactly that reason: without
the pair, a change that is waiting reads as a change that did not work, and
somebody sets it again.

It describes the INSTALLATION — the machine every workspace shares — so it
is the same answer for every tenant and reads no tenant's data.

apiPool.description: The request path's own database connection pool.

executionMode.description: The topology this installation is set to. 'split' runs the API and the executor as two processes, so a fan-out on the executor can never block the request loop; 'combined' runs one process, the pre-split topology. Saved here; it takes effect when the container restarts.
executionMode.title: Executionmode

executionPool.description: The execution path's own pool, deliberately separate from the API's: a fan-out can exhaust this one and the request path keeps all of its own.

executionRole.description: Which half answered this request. In split mode two processes serve the same image, so a reply that does not name its own half cannot be reasoned about.
executionRole.title: Executionrole

isDefault.description: True while nobody has saved a mode; then what the deployment was started with applies.
isDefault.title: Isdefault

restartBlockedReason.description: Null when this installation can restart itself, so the settings above can be collected from here. Otherwise the reason it cannot — shown rather than counted, because a control that refuses without saying why leaves nothing to do next.
restartBlockedReason.title: Restartblockedreason

restartRequired.description: True when the saved mode is not the one running — the change takes effect on the next container restart.
restartRequired.title: Restartrequired

runningExecutionMode.description: What this container is ACTUALLY running right now. Differs from `executionMode` while a saved change waits for a restart.
runningExecutionMode.title: Runningexecutionmode

RuntimeTopologyResponse.title: RuntimeTopologyResponse

RuntimeTopologyUpdate.description:
Body voor ``PATCH /api/v1/platform/runtime``.

De pools stonden hier met opzet NIET in, omdat hun waarden
omgevingsvariabelen zijn en een veld dat niets doet erger is dan geen veld.
Dat argument is vervallen: de supervisor leest de store al vóór hij een
kind spawnt en stelt al elk kind zijn omgeving samen, dus lopen de pools
langs hetzelfde pad als de modus. De prijs is een HERSTART, niet een
uitrol — dezelfde die de sandbox-afmeting hiernaast al betaalt.

Elk veld optioneel: wie alleen de modus zet hoeft de vijf getallen niet mee
te sturen, en omgekeerd. Strict op onbekende sleutels, zodat een typefout
een 422 geeft in plaats van een stil weggegooid veld.

apiMaxOverflow.title: Apimaxoverflow

apiPoolSize.description: Verbindingen die het verzoekpad open houdt.
apiPoolSize.title: Apipoolsize

executionMaxOverflow.description: Extra verbindingen die het uitvoerpad mag openen bij drukte.
executionMaxOverflow.title: Executionmaxoverflow

executionMode.description: 'split' voor twee processen (API en uitvoerder apart), 'combined' voor één. Geldt na een herstart van de container.
executionMode.title: Executionmode

executionPoolSize.description: Verbindingen die het uitvoerpad open houdt.
executionPoolSize.title: Executionpoolsize

executionReserved.description: Verbindingen die het uitvoerpad achterhoudt voor de machinerie die een vastgelopen run herstelt, zodat een fan-out die nooit kan opeten.
executionReserved.title: Executionreserved

RuntimeTopologyUpdate.title: RuntimeTopologyUpdate

van "in gebruik" onderscheiden, en lijkt een wijziging die wacht op een

Response after saving workflow document.

ScopeEdgeSchema.description:
``needer`` cannot land without ``needed``.

What makes the staging list tickable. A commit that writes a process and
leaves its tool behind is complete on the screen and broken in the target
— and nothing goes red there, because the process exists and only refuses
on its first run. So taking one object out has to take everything that
depends on it out with it, and this is the relation that says which.

It describes the WORKSPACE, not the selection: the screen reads it once,
from the whole-workspace preview it makes on mount.
ScopeEdgeSchema.title: ScopeEdgeSchema

ScopeItemSchema.description:
One entity a selection reaches, and what carries it.

``paths`` is empty when nothing can carry it, and ``blocker`` says why:
``not_published`` is the author's to fix, ``unsupported_kind`` is the
format's and nothing the author does today changes it. ``reason`` answers
"why is this in my commit?" for every row — without it a selection is just
a longer list.

SearchPackage.description: A landing with its expansion (§9.1 steps 1 to 3).

SecretPreflightResponse.description:
Required-vs-present secret gap for a config version, before it deploys.

The same computation ``config_import_service._validate_secret_refs`` runs at
deploy time (a missing ``secretRef`` blocks the deploy), surfaced as a
read-only pre-flight so the operator can satisfy the block in-context (#645).
Names + state only — a secret VALUE never appears in this response.

``secrets`` lists every declared ref (present ones first would be arbitrary —
it is name-sorted); ``missing`` is the subset the target vault still lacks
(the block); ``satisfied`` is ``missing == []`` — the deploy may proceed.
SecretPreflightResponse.title: SecretPreflightResponse

SecretRefStatusSchema.description:
One secret the config-to-deploy declares, and what is known about it.

The value is NEVER carried. What IS carried is everything the tree says —
what the credential is for, which kind of auth it is, its non-secret
settings, and which of those settings a connector tool reads out of it. A
checklist of bare names told an operator to create something without
saying what it is, which made the screen a spelling exercise.
SecretRefStatusSchema.title: SecretRefStatusSchema

SecretTransferFile.description: Het hele bestand: een versie, een moment, en de secrets.
SecretTransferFile.title: SecretTransferFile

SecretTransferItem.description:
Eén secret, met zijn waarde.

``value`` is de ONTSLEUTELDE waarde. Hij is optioneel, en dat is met
opzet twee dingen tegelijk: de export zet hem op ``null`` voor een secret
dat niet te ontsleutelen was (met de reden in ``problem``), en de import
leest een ontbrekende waarde als "laat staan wat er is". Zo kun je een
geëxporteerd bestand ook gebruiken om alleen beschrijvingen bij te werken.
SecretTransferItem.title: SecretTransferItem

SecretTransferResult.description: Wat een import deed — geteld, en met de namen die hij raakte.

Insert a published Agent row directly so Playwright specs can
reference it from a workflow's agent step. Mirrors
`_seed_process_owner_agent` from the in-process suite.

Insert a tenant-scoped Flow + one FlowStep so a Playwright spec
can reference a custom exit-tool contract from a workflow's agent
step (e.g. `submit_plan` as the exit tool to exercise V7 §6.3
plan persistence). Mirrors the in-process
``make_single_step_flow`` helper.
SeedFlowRequest.title: SeedFlowRequest

SeedPublishedWorkflowRequest.description:
Mirror of the backend acceptance fixture
``make_published_workflow``: stamps a ``published_document`` onto
the Workflow row directly without going through the publish
validator. Lets Playwright specs seed contract-violating-but-
runnable workflow shapes (e.g. trigger → end with no order field
on edges) the same way the in-process test suite does.

Tied to `is_development`; never exposed in production.
SeedPublishedWorkflowRequest.title: SeedPublishedWorkflowRequest

SeedTestUserRequest.description:
Pre-seed a tenant + user pair for the Playwright suite.

Idempotent: if the user already exists, returns the existing IDs
rather than creating duplicates. The Playwright fixtures call this
once per persona (operator / designer / assignee) and use the
returned ``userId`` as the ``X-Test-User-Id`` header value on all
backend calls (the `dev_auth_bypass` path in
``auth/dependencies.py`` resolves the header into an
``AuthContext``).
SeedTestUserRequest.title: SeedTestUserRequest

SelectTenantRequest.description: Step-2 login payload: pick a tenant from the multi-tenant choice.
SelectTenantRequest.title: SelectTenantRequest

SelectionRootSchema.description:
One thing an author chose to commit.

EVERY kind the file format carries. The screen lists what changed and lets
an author take a line out of the commit, so every changed line has to be
nameable — a changed policy or table too. Four kinds meant the checkbox was
missing on exactly the rows nobody could explain, and the reason lived in a
server-side list the operator could not see.

Absent on purpose: the company (one per workspace, not a line in a list), a
persona (filed under its agent's slug, travels with it) and a secret (a
declaration with no row to name).

``Literal`` rather than a string: an unknown kind is a 422 before any
database read. It is held to :data:`~src.services.config_scope.RootKind` by
``test_the_wire_accepts_exactly_the_kinds_a_commit_can_name``, and the
pair of them is held to the FORMAT by
``test_every_kind_with_a_file_can_be_named`` — being pinned only to
each other let both drift behind the file list at once, which is how a
measure and a query came to have a file nobody could name (#2011).

ServiceTokenListItem.description: A token in the management list — metadata only, never the secret.

One row in a run's session-memory LISTING (#372, #440).

Returned by ``GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/session-memory``. Metadata
only — deliberately no ``content``: serialising every file body just
to draw a list is what made the run Memory panel slow (#440). Fetch a
single file's text from
``GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/session-memory/{file_id}``.

``size_bytes`` is the body's serialised size in octets, so the list
can show how big a file is before anyone opens it. ``tags`` mirrors
the tags stored on the file.

``archived`` says the file was deleted after the fact — it is still
the run's record and still readable, and the panel marks it (#1148).
SessionMemoryFile.title: SessionMemoryFile

SessionMemoryFileContent.description:
One session-memory file WITH its text (#440).

Returned by ``GET /api/v1/runs/{run_id}/session-memory/{file_id}``,
fetched when the operator actually opens a file. ``content`` is the
human-readable text extracted from the file body (``body.markdown``,
then ``body.value``, then a pretty-printed JSON fallback).

SessionMemoryResponse.description: Response for the session-memory listing endpoint (#372).
SessionMemoryResponse.title: SessionMemoryResponse

tenant" line).

One cell somebody answered and has not proposed yet.

Staged values are DURABLE and live on the server, keyed to the branch.
They used to live in the browser, which answered "where does this live
for the next five minutes" rather than "where does it live until it is
finished" — and filling a branch's values takes days and more than one
person.

Because they are shared per branch they are attributed: a second
operator sees whose answer a cell holds before replacing it.

State of a single step within a run.

LARGE and whose declared type is not already object-shaped (#839 S2).
The run-detail route serves the stored form, and a marker is a
three-key object: it validates as-is against ``dict``-typed fields
(``structured_outputs``, ``resolved_inputs``, ``phases``, …) but not
against ``str`` or ``list[...]``, which is where the union earns its
place. A client reads the marker and fetches the body from
``GET /runs/{run_id}/values/{digest}``.

Request body for ``POST /task-queue/stop-bulk``.

``ids`` ONLY — deliberately not the ids-XOR-filter shape the other
bulk actions take. Dismiss-by-filter puts finished rows away;
stop-by-filter would END live work the operator never looked at, and
a mis-aimed filter there reaches a whole workspace's queue. Stopping
is per-selection, on rows somebody chose (#1122).

Aggregate outcome of ``stop-bulk``.

``skipped`` counts rows that had already reached an end — not a
failure, so it must not paint the operator's summary red — and stays
separate from ``errored`` (unknown / cross-tenant / write failed) so
"9 stopped, 3 had already finished" reads honestly.

SyncEnvironmentRequest.description:
``POST /config/environments/sync`` — load this workspace's own branch.

For the environment NO promotion rule advances: the button that says "take
what my branch has now". ``full`` is the one thing it asks, and it asks it
per press because it describes THIS sync: ``true`` means the branch is the
whole configuration, so what it no longer carries leaves the workspace too
(reversibly); ``false`` adds and updates only.

There is no branch, ref or repo field, and that is the point: what gets
loaded is the link the operator set up, never something a request body
names. The same reason ``targetTenantId`` is a guard and not a selector
everywhere else on this surface.
SyncEnvironmentRequest.title: SyncEnvironmentRequest

SystemAdjustments.description:
What the platform changed on its own, in this call (#771).

Two invariants run after every edit and are NOT optional:
``ensure_end_step`` guarantees every step can reach the end point and
wires the edge itself, and ``derive_input_contracts`` projects each
bound input's contract from the output it is bound to. Both are
correct; both used to be invisible, so an author copying one
environment into another found edges they never asked for and
descriptions they never wrote, and could only find them by diffing the
whole document after every call.

Ids and names only — this rides on every mutation response, so it must
stay small. Absent/empty means nothing was adjusted.
SystemAdjustments.title: SystemAdjustments

SystemToolEntry.description: One opt-in system tool the UI can render as a toggle.
SystemToolEntry.title: SystemToolEntry

SystemToolFunctionEntry.description: One function an automation plan step can name as its tool (#1871).
SystemToolFunctionEntry.title: SystemToolFunctionEntry

TableColumnPayload.description:
One column of a table's design, as a client sends it.

``id``, ``name`` and ``label`` are optional because the domain fills
what the author did not type: a name is derived from the label, a
label falls back to the name, and an id is minted once and then kept
(a stored id is what makes a table's payload stable across reads).

choiceOptions.description: The values a choice / multi-choice column may take. Required for those two kinds and meaningless for the others.
choiceOptions.title: Choiceoptions

description.description: What this column means. Mandatory — an agent reads it to know what the column is for, and a save without it is refused.
description.title: Description

id.description: Stable identifier of this column. Omit on a new column — one is minted and kept from then on.
id.title: Id

kind.description: The type of value a cell holds: text, long-text, number, yes-no, date, datetime, time, email, url, choice, multi-choice, object or list. A file is not a cell value and is refused.
kind.title: Kind

label.description: What a person reads at the top of the column.
label.title: Label

name.description: The key this column has in every row, and the identifier tool code refers to. Derived from the label when omitted; never moved by a later label edit.
name.title: Name

required.description: Whether every row must carry a value for this column.
required.title: Required

unique.description: Whether no two rows may hold the same value in this column — a case id, an invoice number. An add or update that would repeat a value is refused, naming the column and the value. Compared the way find compares, so 'C-17' and 'c-17' are the same value; empty cells do not count. Only for text, number, date, datetime, time, email, url and choice columns. schemaBody.description:
The JSON Schema document describing the output contract: `type`, `properties`, `required`, and — the part that is not JSON Schema — `validators`.

`validators` is a list of gates run against a submitted output. Each entry is one of two shapes.

A SHIPPED PREDICATE names `function` (e.g. `validators.min_length`), the `target` field it judges, and its own `args`. Omit `target` to judge the whole output.

A VALIDATOR TOOL names `tool` instead, and gets the STANDARD CALL — every authored validator is invoked the same way, so a screen can offer its inputs and a served spec can describe them:

  `data`    — what the validator is pointed at, untouched. The whole submitted output by default, or the field named by `field`.
  `slots`   — every declared session-memory reference found in `data`, with its text, indexed by the reference itself. The platform resolves these because sandboxed tool code is never handed a lookup callable.
  `binding` — what you declared, verbatim, so the validator knows which values in `data` are references rather than plain values.

Two keys steer it. `field` names the part of the output to hand over; leave it out for the whole output. `slots` lists the fields holding references, e.g. `["key", "source_key"]`. Both are checked on save: a `field` that is not a property, or a `slots` name the rows do not carry, is refused — a name that is not there would never be looked up and the gate would run on unresolved values in silence.

  {"tool": "my.freshness.check", "field": "units", "slots": ["key", "source_key"], "error_message": "REJECTED: {value}"}

A tool MAY instead declare `inputs` — the older, explicit binding, and the way a tool backed by a shipped predicate receives `value` plus its arguments. Each entry is `{"source": "field"|"const", "field": <name>, "as": "slot"?}`; with `as: "slot"` the field's value is read as a reference and the TEXT is passed. `field` may point into a list: `units[].key` is, from every row in `units`, the `key` field. A spec with `inputs` does not get the standard call.

`error_message` is the text an agent sees on refusal; `{value}` is replaced by what the validator reported.
schemaBody.title: Schemabody

ValidatorSpec.description:
One validator attachment — the SINGLE declaration format used at
every level (agent permissions, step contract, schema-bundled).

Mirrors the runtime spec shape documented in
:mod:`src.execution.framework.output_validators`. A spec names its
predicate in ONE of two ways, and each way brings its own binding keys:

  * ``function``     — registry key (e.g. ``validators.min_length``),
                       bound by ``target`` + ``args``
  * ``tool``         — a validator TOOL in the tenant's library, by
                       display name or UUID, bound by ``inputs``
  * ``error_message`` — template fed back to the agent on rejection;
                       the one key both forms share

Exactly one of ``function`` / ``tool``. Naming neither leaves nothing to
run; naming both leaves it unsaid which one does, and a gate does not get
to be ambiguous.

The binding keys do not mix either. The registry path reads ``target``
and ``args`` and never looks at ``inputs``; the tool path reads
``inputs`` and never looks at the other two. Allowing the wrong pair
would persist a key the runtime silently ignores — which is precisely
what ``extra="forbid"`` is here to prevent, so it is enforced rather
than left to the author's memory.

``extra="forbid"``: the UI writes exactly one format; a typo'd key
must fail loudly instead of persisting as a dead key the runtime
silently ignores.

Deliberately NOT camel-aliased: the spec shape is byte-identical at
every level (agent permissions, step contract, schema-bundled), and
step/schema specs live inside verbatim JSONB documents in
snake_case. Aliasing here would make the agent API the one surface
speaking a different dialect.

WorkflowDocumentSchema.description:
Full workflow JSONB document with referential integrity validation.

Validates:
- All step IDs are unique
- All trigger IDs are unique
- Edge from/to reference valid step or trigger IDs

``extra="allow"`` is load-bearing, not decorative (#805). The stored
document is a superset of the four fields validated here — it also carries
column-authoritative metadata (``name``, ``description``, ``stageId``,
``capabilityId``, ``valueStreamId``, ``onFailure``) that rides along on
every read, plus the process's own ``inputs`` and ``constants``.
``PUT /workflows/{id}`` dumps
this model back to a dict before handing it to the service; under the
default ``extra="ignore"`` that dump silently DROPPED every undeclared key,
so the #768 metadata-sync fix and ``_reject_unhonoured_metadata`` — both
reading those keys off the document in the service — could never see them.
Only keys the caller actually sent survive the round-trip, so the service's
"absent key = leave unchanged" contract is preserved. Do NOT narrow this to
an enumerated field list: that reinstates the exact hand-maintained-schema
drift #802/#805 are about.
WorkflowDocumentSchema.title: WorkflowDocumentSchema

get.description: Root endpoint.

post.description: A person says the verdict was right or wrong.

Operator-initiated wake-task plant (#355 Story 4).

Used for force-wakes, dev callback simulation, and recovering a
run from a stuck state. The target run must exist in the caller's
tenant; the idempotency key is mandatory so a refresh / double-
click collapses into ``duplicate`` instead of double-planting.

Errors:
  * 404 — target run missing in this tenant.
  * 422 — unknown ``wake_event_kind``.
  * 409 — idempotency key collides with a still-live row.

patch.description:
Patch ``scheduled_for`` / ``expires_at`` / ``reason`` (#355 Story 4).

All three fields optional; at least one is required (a no-op PATCH
is a 422 so the operator always knows the call produced a change).
Only ``pending`` rows are editable — in-progress / terminal rows
are owned by the queue-tick.

post.description:
Operator-initiated dismissal of a pending wake-task.

Sets the row to ``dead_letter`` with reason ``operator_dismissed``
so the queue-tick stops claiming it and the run's "Waiting for …"
panel no longer surfaces it. The run keeps its current status —
other live wakes (if any) continue.

Validation:
  * 404 if the task does not exist in the caller's tenant.
  * 422 if the row is a spawn-style task (no ``resume_run_id``).
    Spawn-style rows use the existing ``/task-queue/{id}/dismiss``
    inspector path; the dismiss-wake-task surface is wake-only by
    design to keep operator mental models clean.
  * 409 if the row already terminated between fetch + write.

Set ``scheduled_for=now()`` on a pending wake-task (#355 Story 4).

The queue-tick claims it on the next sweep and resumes the targeted
run within the latency floor. The targeted Run stays in ``waiting``
until the queue-tick fires — no immediate status change here.

Errors:
  * 404 — task missing in this tenant.
  * 422 — row is not a wake-task (no ``resume_run_id``) OR not in
    ``pending``.

post.description:
Sign in as a platform administrator on any installation (401 on failure).

What the ``/admin`` screen posts, and the one password path a shut password
door does not close. It needs three secrets together — the installation's
``SETUP_TOKEN``, an address, and that address's own password — and the
account must already administer this installation. Nobody else gets
through, whatever they type.

Public for the same reason as ``/login``: it ESTABLISHES a session, so it
cannot require one. Allowlisted in ``tests/security/test_auth_allowlist.py``
with that reasoning.

It asks nothing about which workspace: there is exactly one it opens, the
hidden platform room the installation is administered from, so a picker
here would be a choice between answers that are all wrong. The union return
type is kept because the client handles both shapes for every door, and a
door that could only ever answer one of them is a door with a narrower
contract than its siblings for no reason a caller can see.

schema.title: Response Admin Login Api V1 Auth Admin Login Post

post.description:
Replace the caller's own password (400 if the current one is wrong).

Returns a FRESH token bundle: the change revokes every session of the
account, and handing the caller a new pair is what keeps the tab they did
it from signed in while every other one is gone.

A wrong current password is **400**, not 401: the session is still valid,
so a client that signs people out on 401 must not do so for a typo. On
this route 401 means only that the session itself has gone.

Ask for a reset link. Always 202, always the same message.

Known address, unknown address, suspended member, removed member: one
status and one body. The service decides whether anything is actually
sent and says nothing about it — see
:meth:`AuthService.request_password_reset` for the timing equalisation
that keeps the two branches indistinguishable in the clock as well.

Copy a live session into a new, independent one (401 if stale).

What a new browser tab calls: every tab holds a session of its own, and
a new one starts as a copy of the session the person used last.

Verify credentials, then either return a token bundle or, when the
credential belongs to several tenants, a tenant choice (401 on failure).

Make a workspace from the sign-in picker, and enter it.

The way out of holding none. Authorised by the continuation token rather
than a session, because the caller has none — see
``AuthService.create_workspace_from_selection`` for why that keeps the
session invariant intact. The token says who; only a platform
administrator may.

post.description: Rotate the refresh token and return a fresh bundle (401 if stale).

Redeem a reset link and set a new password (400 if it is spent).

Validate JWT and return user context.

Called by the frontend on app load to verify the session
and get tenant/user info.

Claim a fresh installation: create its first workspace and owner.

Open only while the installation has no accounts at all, and only to the
holder of its ``SETUP_TOKEN``. 410 once claimed — the door is spent, not
refused. See ``AuthService.complete_setup`` for why the order of those two
checks matters.

Give an existing account the administration of this installation.

The other first-run door: open only while the install has people in it and
nobody able to run it, and only to the holder of its ``SETUP_TOKEN``. 410
once somebody administers it — the door is spent, not refused.

204 and no body, deliberately. The caller holds a deployment variable, not
somebody's password; they sign in afterwards as themselves. See
``AuthService.claim_platform_administration``.
Register a new tenant + owner user and return a token bundle.

get.description:
Which sign-in methods this installation offers, and whether it has one.

Read by the sign-in screen before it draws anything, so it can show the
Microsoft button, the password form, both — or, on an installation nobody
has claimed yet, the first-run form instead.

``setup_required`` costs one ``EXISTS`` against ``accounts``. It tells an
anonymous caller that this install has never been set up, which is a fact
they would learn by trying the setup endpoint anyway, and which the screen
genuinely needs in order to draw itself. What protects an unclaimed install
is the token's strength, which is why a short one is refused at boot.

Start a sign-in attempt: the directory's authorize URL.

Each call mints a fresh signed state, so the URL is for one attempt. It
hands out no secret — the state is a signed nonce, and the PKCE verifier it
implies never leaves this server — which is why the route needs no session
of its own.

An installation with no directory configured gets a refusal, not a 500.

post.description:
Complete a sign-in: verify the directory's token, then find the seat.

Two separate questions, answered in this order and by different layers:

1. Who is this? — the ``id_token`` must verify against this installation's
   directory binding (401 if not).
2. Do they hold a seat? — their address must match a membership an
   administrator created (403 if not). Signing in never creates one.

Answers exactly like ``POST /api/v1/auth/login``: a token bundle, or a
workspace choice when the credential holds several memberships — so the
client's sign-in handling is the same code for both doors.

unless they are asked: what ONE ROW of its result is.

Served rather than documented, for the same reason as the placement

standard, and a copy in another repo drifts.

get.description:
What this start decided on each beat, and why — newest first.

Any member may read it, like Schedules: everyone may see what starts by
itself, and a "no" repeated for days is exactly what they need to see.

The chain and the side branches of this workspace's connected repo.

One read for the whole tab: the chain in manifest order with each link's
state toward the next environment, every side branch with its two distances
to its stem, and the per-environment source policy (B16).

Returns ``{overview: null, allowedSources: []}`` when nothing is connected
or the GitHub App is not configured — the UI shows its connect call to
action rather than an error. Admin-only, tenant-scoped through the F1
binding.

post.description:
Cut a side branch off the chain, from a branch that exists.

The name is validated before it can ever become a path segment at the
provider (422); an unknown source branch is a 404 and an existing name a
409. Returns the new branch as the tab draws it — zero ahead, zero behind,
with the branch it sprang from as its stem. Audited.

Bring the stem's commits into side branch ``branch``.

The button under "two commits of main are not in here". Only ever for a
side branch: a chain branch catches up by being promoted into (409). A
branch that is already level is a no-op that says so. Audited.

Throw side branch ``branch`` away.

Refused (409) for a chain branch, for the branch THIS workspace stands on,
and — without ``confirmUnmerged`` — for a branch that still carries work its
stem does not have. That last refusal names the number of commits at stake,
so the screen can ask a question instead of shrugging. Audited.

Point THIS environment at ``branch`` — the way to try a version out.

A production-designated environment runs its own branch and nothing else
(409): one road to production, and it is promotion along the chain. Setting
it back to its own branch is allowed, because that ends a detour rather
than starting one. A manifest may narrow it further per environment with
``allowedBranches`` (409 naming the policy). The branch must exist and
carry a manifest (422), the same bar a connect sets. Audited.

Merge ``branch`` into ``into`` by merging the pull request that is open.

The direction is not negotiable: a chain branch may only go to the next
environment down the chain, a side branch only back into its own stem, and
anything else is a 409. With no open pull request it is a 404 — open one
first, so the change is reviewed where it is reviewed (B6). Audited.
Atomically stage a reviewed bundle as target-tenant drafts only.
Compare target drafts with the portable source without mutating either.
Validate a portable tree before any draft-migration write is possible.
Statically validate tools and target bindings without execution.

get.description:
The connected repo's environments + promotion state, chain-ordered.

Resolves the tenant's connected repo through the #549-F1 verified binding
and reads each environment's branch head live. Returns ``{environments: []}``
when nothing is connected or the GitHub App is not configured (the UI shows
the connect CTA rather than an error). Admin-only.

post.description:
Fast-forward-promote ``from`` into ``to`` on the connected repo.

Advances the ``to`` environment's branch to the ``from`` environment's
commit iff that move is a fast-forward — a diverged / behind target is a 409
("reconcile upstream; do not force"), never a force move. The promotion is
audited. Returns the refreshed environment list. Admin-only; scoped to the
caller's own tenant via the F1 binding.

Load the configuration version this workspace ran BEFORE this one (B9).

**The body names nothing.** The commit is resolved server-side from this
workspace's own audit trail, so the button can only ever do what it says;
a request that could name a ref would be a deploy endpoint wearing the
word "rollback", and the audit line would inherit that lie.

It is a normal deploy of an older commit — same import, same gates, same
``config_deployed`` line — with one extra row saying it was a step
BACKWARDS and from where. Which means the version you are leaving becomes
the "previous" one, and pressing it again returns: correct, and visible.

get.description:
What "Terug naar vorige versie" would restore, before it is pressed.

A button that says what it will do before it does it — the version is on
the screen, so the operator is choosing a commit rather than trusting a
word.

What every environment of THIS customer says it is running.

Each manifest environment is asked over its own public ``/health`` — the
only channel B8 allows between two workspaces, and the reason no credential
is needed for any of them. The answer (a status and a short sha) is laid
against that environment's branch, so the row can say "identical" or "two
commits behind" rather than just "up".

Never partial and never fatal: an environment that is silent, has no address
or declares an address that is not a public origin each get a row saying
which of those it is. The sweep is parallel and bounded — B-NB4/B-NB6: this
route waits on the network, so it may not wait on it one environment at a
time.

Returns ``{environments: [], checkedAt}`` when nothing is connected or the
GitHub App is not configured — the same graceful empty as the list, so the
screen shows its connect call to action instead of an error. Admin-only,
scoped to the caller's own tenant through the #549-F1 binding.

post.description:
Load this workspace's own linked branch into it, on request.

The button for the environment nothing promotes into. ``full`` is the
operator's answer to "everything, or only what changed" — asked per press
rather than stored, because it is what THIS sync should do.

An INTERACTIVE ADMIN SESSION is what makes an explicit ``full`` legitimate:
it is a person answering, not a request body asking for deletions. Every
other deploy path leaves the answer to the workspace's own stored setting,
so a deploy credential can never ask for removals (#616 C2 still applies on
top — a protected environment takes an admin session, which this is).

Refused (422) when a promotion rule owns this environment: that one is
advanced by promoting its source into it. Returns the deploy's own summary,
``removed`` included — a sync that deletes says so in its result.

Remove the object from the branch and from this workspace. Audited.

Only the files this object renders as are touched: a removal is not a
commit of the workspace that happens to be missing something. The service
re-plans and refuses on any blocker before the first write of either kind —
a dependant, the platform's own, or a branch that does not carry the
object — each as a sentence the screen can print.

What taking this object out of the branch would do. Writes nothing.

Answers the three things the dialog must show before anybody confirms:
which files leave, what still points at the object, and what each
environment of the chain sees. A refusal is part of the answer, not an
error — the plan comes back with ``allowed: false`` and a sentence per
reason, because an operator sent away with a status code has been told
nothing.

Dry-run a config version against the caller's tenant (#548).

Accepts EITHER ``files`` (a posted ``{path: content}`` tree — CI / the app
after serializing, kept for back-compat) OR ``ref`` (+ ``refKind``), a
branch/tag of the tenant's CONNECTED repo the backend fetches (#549 F1)
before diffing. Returns a per-entity, field-level diff — created / changed /
unchanged / deleted — plus a summary and a ``planId`` the frontend echoes
back on publish so the commit applies exactly what was previewed. Nothing is
applied; a re-plan of an unchanged tree reports no changes.

The answer also carries the ``aftercare``: what the deploy would leave for a
human, computed from the SAME version it just diffed (see
:func:`_aftercare`). A ``blocking`` line is the screen's refusal to deploy.

Aborts 404 if the tenant is unknown or no repo is connected, and 422 (naming
the offending key) on an unsupported schema or a dangling reference — the
same loud failures a deploy would hit, surfaced before anything is applied.

Add a missing secret to the caller's own vault, inline in the deploy flow.

The write half of the guided fill-in (#645): delegates to the SAME
:meth:`SecretService.create_secret` the general secrets surface uses (Fernet
encryption, duplicate-name guard, audited fact-only — key name + auth type,
NEVER the value), so no new storage or business logic is introduced. Scoped
to ``auth.tenant_id`` (never a body-supplied tenant), so an admin can only
ever set THEIR OWN environment's value — there is no cross-environment path.

Admin-only — a stricter gate than the general secrets route, because adding a
credential mid-deploy is an admin action. The value is never echoed back:
the response carries only the new secret's id, name, auth type, and version.

Which secrets a config version needs, and which the target vault lacks.

The read-only pre-flight behind the guided fill-in (#645): accepts the SAME
body as ``/config/plan`` — EITHER a posted ``files`` tree OR a ``ref`` of the
tenant's connected repo the backend fetches (#549 F1) — and returns every
``secretRef`` the config declares tagged present/missing against the caller's
OWN vault. A secret VALUE is never returned. Scoped to ``auth.tenant_id`` (the
deploy target is always the caller's own workspace), so one environment can
never probe another's vault. Admin-only.

Aborts 404 if no repo is connected (ref path) and 422 on an unsupported
schema or a dangling reference — the same loud failures a deploy would hit,
surfaced before anything is applied.

get.description:
The connected repo's loadable source refs — one per manifest environment.

Resolves the tenant's connected repo through the #549 F1 verified binding
and maps each live ``axonity.yaml`` environment to a selectable branch ref.
Returns ``[]`` when nothing is connected or the GitHub App is not configured
(the UI shows the connect CTA rather than an error). Admin-only.

schema.title: Response List Config Sources Api V1 Config Sources Get

get.description:
Every value the connected branch declares, per environment.

One read of one branch answers the whole screen: the grid, which cells block
a deploy (B18), which rows need looking at (B19) and which values have lost
their declaration (B20). No environment's workspace is asked anything — the
values live in the branch, which is the same boundary the ping draws for
deploy state (B8).

The answer also names the proposal a commit would JOIN, when there is one,
so the screen can ask which review this change belongs in BEFORE it writes
— after the commit is after the choice.

Returns ``{connected: false}`` with everything empty when nothing is
connected or the GitHub App is not configured, so the screen shows its
connect call to action rather than an error. Admin-only.

post.description:
Write this screen's edits and decisions to the branch as ONE commit.

Decisions are carried out before edits: a decision answers what the branch
already said, an edit is the operator's new answer, and an answer typed on
the screen must win over a notice resolved on the same press.

A press that changes nothing commits nothing — ``commitSha`` comes back
``null`` with an empty ``files``. An empty pull request that reads as
"saved" is the worst of both answers, and so is the commit equivalent.

Refused (422) when nothing is connected, when a named environment is not in
the manifest, or when a key is not a value. The branch move itself is
fast-forward-only at the provider: a branch that moved under this press is
rejected, never forced.

delete.description: Put one value back on the screen. Idempotent.

put.description:
Take one value off this branch's screen.

Adding an object brings ALL its fields — a workflow's eight constants, a
connector's settings — and usually two of them matter on this branch.
Hiding the rest says "we are not touching this one here".

It is not an answer and not "inherit the default": nothing about what a
deploy carries changes. And it cannot conceal one either — a value an
environment states, or that has something staged, is shown whatever this
says.

delete.description:
Take one object off this branch's list.

It removes nothing an environment states and nothing staged: the object
simply stops being shown. Idempotent — taking off what is not on the list
is the outcome the caller asked for.

put.description:
Put one object on this branch's values list.

A branch declares far more than anyone wants to see at once, so the
screen shows what this workspace decided about and an operator adds the
objects they are going to answer. That choosing is the first half of the
work and on a big branch the slower half — so it is kept, like the
answers themselves. Adding the same object twice is the same list.

delete.description:
Throw away one typed answer that was never proposed.

Idempotent: dropping a cell that holds nothing is the outcome the caller
asked for, not an error, and two operators clearing the same cell must
not give the second one a failure.

put.description:
Save one typed answer without proposing it.

The screen's two verbs are different intentions and this is the quiet
one. Committing opens or extends a pull request on the configuration
repository — half an answer does not belong in one — while filling a
branch's values takes days and more than one person.

The answer is kept against the branch the screen is looking at, because
a value key need not exist on another one. It is shared with everyone
who can open this screen, which is the handover the whole feature is
for, and it records who answered so the next operator can see whose
answer they are replacing.

The environment is resolved against the manifest, so a typo cannot
create a file for an environment the chain does not declare. Admin-only.

Save a whole set of answers without proposing them — all or nothing.

What "copy one environment's values to another" sends. One request, so a
copy of forty cells is not forty round-trips; and one transaction, so a
copy either lands whole or not at all — half a copy is an environment
that is neither the old one nor the copy, and nobody can tell which cells

post.description:
Deploy a config version using a per-environment deploy credential (CI).

Authenticated by the ``X-Deploy-Token`` header (not a session), rate-limited
per IP AND per credential, and hard-scoped: the target tenant is the
credential's ONE tenant, so a credential for env A can never deploy env B (an
explicit mismatching ``targetTenantId`` is a 403). Refused (503, audited) when
the kill-switch is off.

A credential can NEVER deploy a PROTECTED (production) environment (#616 C2):
that takes an interactive admin session, so this path is refused (403,
audited) — deploy production from the app. Ordinary environments are
unaffected.

Deliberately does NOT plan-pin (``expected_plan_id=None``): a pipeline has no
interactive "review the plan, then publish" step — the review gate for CI is
the PR + CI plan-preview BEFORE merge (#548), not a per-request hash echo. The
``expectedPlanId`` field is honored only on the admin ``/deploy`` path.

Dry-run a config file-tree using a per-environment deploy credential (CI).

The read-only counterpart of ``/ci/deploy``: authenticated by the SAME
``X-Deploy-Token`` credential (constant-time, scoped to the credential's ONE
tenant — an explicit mismatching ``targetTenantId`` is a 403), rate-limited on
the same per-IP + per-credential budget, and delegated to the SAME
``ConfigPlanService`` (#548) the app's session-authed ``/api/v1/config/plan``
uses — so a CI plan is byte-identical to the in-app preview. The target tenant
is ALWAYS the credential's tenant, never a body-supplied one.

Deliberately NOT kill-switched (``CONFIG_IMPORT_ENABLED``): a plan writes no
config, so it must keep working even when deploys to the environment are
frozen — this is the review gate CI runs on a PR (validate + plan) before a
merge triggers the (kill-switchable) deploy. Read-only: nothing is applied.

Commit the caller tenant's active config to a connected repo as a PR.

Serializes the ACTIVE config (#546 — secret-free + fail-closed), resolves
the target repo on the caller's VERIFIED installation bindings (#549 F1),
then creates a branch, batch-commits the file-tree, and opens a PR against
the repo's default branch (#549 provider). Admin-only; the commit is
audited. A provider fault surfaces as a sanitised 502, an unconnected repo
as a 404, and a secret-shaped value aborts (422) before any Git write.

With a ``selection`` only the chosen agents' and processes' files are
written and every other file in the repository is left alone; without one
the whole workspace is committed, as before.

What committing would CHANGE in the repository — without writing it.

The screen an author decides from and the commit that follows answer from
the same plan, so they cannot disagree about which files are touched or
what happens to each. Without a ``selection`` this previews the WHOLE
workspace commit, which is the one an author reaches for most.

It DOES call the provider — a comparison has to read the repository — but
only to list the tree, and it writes nothing: no branch, no commit, no pull
request, so an author may look as often as they like. Scoped to the
caller's OWN workspace (``auth.tenant_id``, never the body); the repo is
re-authorized against the caller's verified bindings, so an unconnected one
is a 404.

B-NB8, the nested case: ``files`` / ``carried`` / ``notCarried`` are not
paged, and are bounded by the workspace's own entity count rather than by
machine activity — a commit can never touch more than the files an author's
entities render as. Each row is O(1) in size (a path, a word, a name),
which is the property that matters: nothing here grows with what an agent
DID. Paging is also the wrong shape for this answer — the caller asked what
one commit would change, and half of that is not an answer.

Verify GitHub's post-authorize redirect and link the admin's identity.

All verification (signature, expiry, single-use nonce, tenant+user match)
and the encrypted token exchange happen in the service layer. The connection
is audited — the FACT only, never the token. Admin-only.

Connect a visible repo — bind-then-connect from OAuth authority (#630 1b).

Option 1: the admin installed the App on GitHub directly, so connecting
establishes the tenant's installation binding from the admin's OWN verified
OAuth access — no signed Axonity install link. In order:

1. Re-verify (service) the ``installationId`` against the admin's user token
   — a client-passed id is NEVER trusted (403 if the admin can't access it).
2. Establish/guard the binding (service): new → created + audited; already
   this tenant's → idempotent; another tenant's → 409 (anti-hijack, #549).
3. Connect on the CHOSEN branch — ``connect_on_branch``, not ``connect``:
   the picker (#630 step 2) lets the admin pick ANY existing branch, which
   need not be the repo's default (e.g. ``main`` is app code, ``sandbox`` is
   config) — gating on default-branch compliance would 404 a perfectly
   valid non-default branch. Compliance is enforced on the branch actually
   being linked; the user OAuth token still grants NO connect/deploy
   authority (App installation token, unchanged).

A production-designated environment stays gated on an interactive admin
session (#616 C2), unchanged. Admin-only; both the bind and the connect are
audited.

Make a non-compliant visible repo compliant, then connect it (#630 2a).

For a repo the admin can see but which has no ``axonity.yaml``: re-verify the
``installationId`` against the admin's OWN OAuth token + bind from that
authority (403 if inaccessible, 409 anti-hijack), DIRECT-COMMIT the scaffold
to a FRESH branch (never a PR, never the default/existing branches), and link
the repo on that branch through the App installation token (binding-gated).

An already-compliant repo skips the SCAFFOLD — it has its manifest already —
but still honours a named ``branch``, cutting it from the default when it
does not exist yet. This used to read "skips the scaffold" full stop, while
the code also dropped the requested branch and connected the default; a
named environment then landed on trunk and its manifest entry replaced the
one already there.

The user OAuth token grants no connect/deploy authority. Admin-only; the
bind, scaffold and connect are each audited.

no cross-tenant rebind) and auditing happen in the service layer.

Receive + verify a GitHub App webhook delivery, then dispatch a push.

Verifies the HMAC signature over the RAW body FIRST (an unset secret or a
missing/invalid signature is rejected). A verified ``push`` to a linked
branch becomes a gated deploy trigger (#616 C4): auto-deploy for a
non-protected ``auto_deploy`` link, an approval-gated proposal for a
protected one, a no-op for an unlinked branch — idempotent on the delivery
id, and pinned to the pushed commit (``after``). Every other event — and a
branch DELETE, which GitHub sends as a push with the same ``refs/heads/*``
ref shape — is acknowledged only.

Returns 202 once the push is handled or ignored. A TRANSIENT provider fault
is deliberately NOT caught: it surfaces as a 5xx so the delivery (and its
idempotency claim) rolls back and GitHub redelivers, rather than 202-ing a
deploy that silently never happened.

The webhook SECRET is resolved DB-first (env-fallback) BEFORE verification,
because a self-hosted App (#616 C5) keeps its secret in ``github_app_config``
with the env var unset — it is needed to verify at all. That one query sits
behind the per-IP invalid-delivery throttle, so it can't be flooded. The
heavier PROVIDER resolution stays LAZY — only for a validated ``push``,
AFTER the signature check — so a rejected delivery never triggers it.

Welke modellen deze installatie kent, hoe ze bereikt worden, wat ze kosten.

Eén lezing voor het hele scherm: de catalogus met per model zijn routes,
de prijs die NU geldt met alle prijzen die eraan voorafgingen, de tiers van
de installatie, en welke modellen nog geen prijs hebben.

Installatiebreed — hetzelfde antwoord voor elke werkruimte. De WAARDE van
een modelsleutel staat er nooit in: alleen de naam, of hij gezet is, sinds
wanneer, en welke routes hem gebruiken (#1810).

post.description:
Zet een model in de tabel, met zijn route én zijn prijs.

Eén handeling, drie rijen eronder: de catalogus zegt WAT het model is, de
route hoe we hem bellen, de prijsrij wat hij kost en vanaf wanneer. Dat
splitsen zou een model opleveren dat bestaat en niet aan te roepen is —
precies de stand die dit scherm wegneemt. De prijs is daarom verplicht.

delete.description: Haal een modelsleutel weg — geweigerd zolang een route hem gebruikt.

put.description:
Zet of vervang één modelsleutel van de installatie (#1810).

Alleen een platformbeheerder: de sleutel bepaalt over wiens account elke
modelaanroep loopt, en een klant mag dat niet kunnen veranderen. De waarde
gaat versleuteld de kluis van de installatie in en komt nooit terug —
niet in dit antwoord, niet in de audit.

patch.description:
Verbeter een prijsrij ter plekke: een TYPFOUT, geen nieuw tarief.

Het verschil is niet cosmetisch. Een nieuw tarief krijgt een eigen periode
omdat het oude getal echt gegolden heeft; een typfout heeft nooit voor
iets gegolden, en daar een periode voor verzinnen zou zeggen van wel.

Het is ook de manier om een prijs te laten AFLOPEN zonder opvolger: zet
``validTo``. Het model heeft dan geen prijs meer, wat het scherm hardop
zegt en de runtime weigert te gokken.

Pas aan HOE een model bereikt wordt: kluisitem, endpoint, aan of uit.

De prijs zit hier niet bij. Die heeft een periode, en een nieuw tarief
sluit het vorige af in plaats van het te overschrijven — een aparte
handeling, hieronder.

post.description:
Een nieuw tarief vanaf ``validFrom``; het vorige wordt afgesloten.

De oude rij blijft staan met de periode waarin hij gold. Dat is wat een
run van vorige maand navertelbaar houdt tegen het bedrag waarmee hij
werkelijk is gerekend — precies wat verloren ging toen een prijs nog drie
kolommen op de route was die je overschreef.

put.description:
Zet de tiers van deze installatie: namen, modellen én VOLGORDE.

De hele lijst in één keer, want de volgorde is deel van de waarde: een
tier omhoog schuiven is geen bewerking van één rij. Het is ook wat
toevoegen, hernoemen en verwijderen tot dezelfde handeling maakt.

Vier tiers zijn wat er MEEKOMT, niet wat er mag bestaan. Een werkruimte
mag er nog steeds van afwijken.

Geweigerd zolang een tier erop draait: een tier zonder model lost bij het
DRAAIEN op tot niets, en dan is de run de plek waar iemand het ontdekt.

The workspace is the caller's own, from the auth context: a platform

get.description:
What this installation is actually running.

The three facts that decide whether a stuck run is a bug or a topology:
whether the API/executor split is on, which half answered, and how many
database connections each half may hold.

Alles hier is een INSTELLING: de uitvoeringsmodus en de vijf poolgetallen
worden opgeslagen en gelden na een herstart, want de supervisor leest ze
bij het opstarten. Het antwoord draagt daarom allebei — wat er is
opgeslagen én wat dit proces werkelijk vasthoudt.

Leest geen gegevens van een werkruimte: dit beschrijft de machine die elke
werkruimte deelt, en het is voor allemaal hetzelfde antwoord.

patch.description:
Zet de topologie en de poolgrootten van deze installatie.

Allebei gelden na een HERSTART, en om dezelfde reden: de supervisor
beslist bij het opstarten hoeveel kinderen hij spawnt en met welke
omgeving, en een draaiend proces verandert daar niet meer van. Het
antwoord draagt daarom per pool wat er is opgeslagen naast wat dit proces
werkelijk vasthoudt.

De pools stonden hier eerst niet in, met het argument dat hun waarden
omgevingsvariabelen zijn. Dat argument is vervallen zodra de supervisor de
store leest — zie ``services/connection_pools.py``.

Elk veld optioneel: wie alleen de modus zet, hoeft de getallen niet mee te
sturen. Wat niet meekomt blijft staan.

Op dezelfde poort als de GET — `require_platform_admin`. Dit beschrijft
niet hoeveel één werkruimte mag pakken maar HOE de machine draait die ze
allemaal delen.

post.description:
Herstart deze installatie, zodat de opgeslagen instellingen gelden.

De twee instellingen hierboven gelden "na een herstart", en tot nu was een
herstart het enige wat je niet in het product kon doen: je sloeg een
beslissing op en moest hem buiten het product ophalen. Dit sluit dat gat.

Het is geen nieuw mechanisme: de supervisor heeft met wat hem draait al de
afspraak dat een niet-nul exit "start me opnieuw" betekent, dus stopt dit
proces zichzelf met de code die hij herkent en komt de container terug —
waarbij hij de store opnieuw leest. Geen console, geen platform-API, geen
inloggegevens.

**Antwoordt eerst, stopt daarna.** Het proces dat dit verzoek bedient is
het proces dat stopt, dus wordt het stoppen een moment vooruit gezet; wie

post.description:
Stop a selection of runs — administrators only (epic #744).

Changing the workspace's queue is an operator action, so this is
gated on ``require_admin``; a member who wants to stop their OWN run
uses ``POST /runs/{run_id}/cancel``, which allows admin-or-creator.

Per-run outcomes are tallied (``cancelled`` / ``alreadyTerminal`` /
``errored``) rather than aborting the batch on the first problem —
an operator stopping 20 runs must not be blocked by one that
finished a second earlier.

**Unlike ``/runs/bulk/archive`` this is NOT a single-commit route.**
``RunService.bulk_stop`` commits after every run because cancelling
takes advisory ``xact`` locks on the run and all its descendants, and
those are only released by a real commit — batching them into one
transaction can exhaust the cluster-wide lock table (see the
``bulk_stop`` docstring). The ``commit()`` below therefore only
persists the ``runs_bulk_stopped`` summary audit event; it is kept
because the route, not the service, owns that final boundary.

get.description:
What this tenant's run history costs, split by retention class.

Admin-gated: it reports the tenant's total data footprint, which is
operational information rather than something a member needs to do
their work.

The split is the point (#863). Retention keeps CONVERSATIONS forever
and expires the OPERATIONAL payload, so a single total tells an
operator nothing about what setting a horizon would reclaim — and the
two are NOT separable from table sizes, because ``run_values`` holds
both a step's fetched dataset and, since #853, an externalised
transcript.

Declared BEFORE ``/runs/{run_id}`` — FastAPI matches in declaration
order, and "storage" would otherwise be parsed as a run id and
rejected as a malformed UUID.

One page of the steps waiting on a human (epic #811 S5).

Paged over the waiting RUNS, not over the to-do items: the cursor
names a position in ``(created_at, id)``, which is a run's
coordinates. One waiting run can carry several waiting steps, so
``items`` may outnumber ``pageSize`` — ``pageSize`` bounds what was
read, which is what keeps the response bounded.

A fan-out can park thousands of items on a manual step at once, and
nothing bounds how long they wait, so this list needs its
continuation marker as much as the run list does.

post.description: Archive a run (hide from default view).

Accept a cancel request for a running or waiting run.

**#725 — this ACCEPTS and returns; it does not wait for the cascade.**
The heavy lineage work (descendant walk, bulk settles, cost roll-up,
memory cleanup — seconds on a large FOR EACH) is drained on the
executor from a durable ``task_queue`` job, off this event loop. The
run in this response is therefore still non-terminal, with
``cancelRequestedAt`` set; ``status='cancelled'`` lands moments later
over Realtime. Clients render "Cancelling…" from
``cancelRequestedAt`` rather than assume a terminal status came back.

Deliberately NOT admin-gated: stopping a run you started is an
ordinary member's right and the run-detail page offers it. The rule
— **administrator OR the run's creator** — is enforced inside
``RunService.request_cancel`` so every caller inherits it; a third
party gets 403. A run with no creator (cron / webhook) is admin-only.
Cancelling an already-terminal run stays a 422.

Resume a parked conversation from an inbound channel reply (#777 S5).

PUBLIC of a *user session* — there is deliberately no ``get_auth_context``
dependency, because an email / WhatsApp adapter has none. It is not open:
three checks stand in for one, in this order.

1. **Who is calling** (#988) — the adapter presents its own credential.
   Without this the ``sender`` below is caller-asserted and proves nothing.
2. **How often** (#986) — rate-limited per IP and per secret before any
   database work, the same treatment ``POST /api/v1/triggers/{token}`` has
   had since security M3, and for the same two reasons: an unauthenticated
   caller must not hammer the run lookup, and a leaked secret must not
   churn runs.
3. **Whether this reply is genuine** (#986) — the channel binding on the
   wait: the secret we sent, and the address we sent it to. See
   ``RunService.post_channel_reply`` and ``services/channel_binding.py``.

Mirrors the message route's two-commit durability.

get.description:
Per-state row counts for a FOR EACH batch on this run.

Drives the run-page children-progress badge so operators see
``12 / 1500 succeeded · 3 failed · 1485 pending`` rather than an
opaque "Waiting for children…". Frontend polls this while the
fanning-out step is ``running``.

Two-layer tenant scoping: ``run_service.get_run`` confirms the
run belongs to the caller's tenant (raises 404 otherwise), and
``task_queue_service.batch_progress`` filters rows by tenant_id
so a forged ``batch_id`` from another tenant returns all-zero
counts. The ``run_id`` itself is not used in the count query —
it's only here for URL lineage + the implicit auth check.

One agent invocation's transcript, on open (#875).

``GET /runs/{run_id}`` lists every invocation with its metadata and a
``messageCount``; this serves the conversation behind one of those
rows. Before it existed, the run page downloaded every transcript in
the run to draw a list — 287,416 B of a 307,069 B response on run
``369e81be``, none of it displayed until an operator opened a step.

Same contract as ``GET /runs/{run_id}/values/{digest}`` (#839 S2) and
``GET /runs/{run_id}/session-memory/{file_id}`` (#440): a collection
view carries handles, a body transfers when someone asks for it.

404s unless the run belongs to the caller's tenant AND the invocation
belongs to THAT run — an invocation id observed elsewhere reads
nothing here.

One page of a launch's ITEM RESULTS, newest first (epic #811 S3).

The inside of a launch: one row per item its FOR EACH processed, in the
same page envelope and with the same cursor rule as the launch list
that got the operator here (``GET /workflows/{id}/runs``). Each row's
``id`` is a real run — open it for that one item's full detail.

``outcome`` is answered by the DATABASE. That is the point of the
parameter: on a 4,415-item launch the twelve failures are scattered
through the middle, so a client filtering what it has downloaded would
show an operator nothing and call it "no failures".

``step_id`` is how ONE group is opened (#1527). A run can hold several
groups, and sending the reader to the launch-wide list shows them
another group's items under this group's heading — which is worse than
showing nothing, because nothing says so.

A launch that never fanned out returns an empty last page — never a
cursor that keeps a scrolling client asking.

Everything that happened, nested at the depth it happened: the run,
its steps, and the items a fan-out step handed out. Flat, with parent

This is the surface the run page STREAMS. It carries no bodies, so its
size follows the run's shape rather than its content: one realtime
tick costs the same for a launch over four thousand items as for one
over four, where refetching the run detail costs the whole document.

``item_cap`` bounds the items listed per fan-out step; the rest are
counted in that step's ``counts.truncated`` and live on the paged
item-results surface. Nothing is truncated in silence.

Tenant isolation: the service's run pre-check 404s a run the caller
cannot see, and every query beneath it filters by ``tenant_id``.

The items one fan-out step handed out, beyond what the outline listed.

The outline is what the run page STREAMS, so it stays bounded: it lists
``item_cap`` items per step and counts the rest. Counting them is only
half an answer — a step that says "121 not listed" and offers no way
onward is a dead end for the reader who came looking for item 40.

This is that way onward. Same nodes as the outline's own — the item AND
the steps beneath it — and the same order, which is what makes ``offset``
exact: carry on at the number the outline stopped at and no item comes
round twice or falls between two stretches.

Deliberately NOT part of the streamed surface. A realtime tick keeps
costing what the run's shape costs, however much a reader has expanded.

Tenant isolation: the service's run pre-check 404s a run the caller

post.description:
Re-dispatch a stuck run — administrators only (epic #744).

For a run sitting in a non-terminal status that nothing is driving —
typically ``pending`` after a backend restart. The run is put back on
the RunQueue and resumes from its own step states; no new run is
created. ``RunService.restart_run`` owns the mechanics (it reuses the
orphan-recovery rewind) and the idempotency decision.

Returns ``already_active`` — a no-op, nothing enqueued — when a
worker currently owns the run, so a double-click cannot double-
advance it. A terminal run is rejected with 422; an unknown or
cross-tenant run with 404.

A run PARKED on an open wait marker is also rejected with 422: it is
suspended by design and belongs to its wake ticket, not to this
endpoint (``SUSPEND-RESUME-DESIGN.md`` §2). The message points the
operator at the wake controls. A ``waiting`` run with no open marker
is the genuinely stranded case and restarts normally.

get.description:
List a run's session-memory files — metadata only (#372, #440).

Returns the title, kind, tags, size and timestamp of every file the
agent wrote to session memory during this run. Bodies are NOT
included: serialising up to 200 full JSONB bodies just to draw a list
is what made the Memory panel slow (#440). Fetch a single file's text
from ``GET /runs/{run_id}/session-memory/{file_id}``.

A file archived after the run ended is listed with ``archived:
true`` rather than omitted (#1148) — this is the run's record, and
the runs whose notes were wiped by the old terminal cleanup are
exactly the ones a post-mortem opens.

Tenant isolation is enforced in the service (run pre-check, then
tenant-scoped folder and file queries). Returns an empty list when no
session folder exists yet.

Fetch one session-memory file's text, on open (#440).

The listing counterpart to ``GET /runs/{run_id}/session-memory``.
404s unless the run belongs to the caller's tenant, the file belongs
to the caller's tenant, AND the file lives in THIS run's session
folder — so a file id borrowed from another run is not readable here.

An archived file is served (#1148): those three checks are what makes
the read safe, and being soft-deleted was never one of them.

post.description:
Submit an answer to an ask_user-suspended step.

Epic #353 — the answer no longer mutates the run directly. The
service plants a wake-task (``wake_event_kind=user_answer``,
``priority=100``, ``scheduled_for=now()``); the row is committed
durably here, then dispatched in-process so the operator sees an
immediate resume. On any dispatch-side exception the wake-task
remains pending and the queue-tick's stale-claim sweep recovers
it within ~10 minutes — closing the historical "crashed between
answer-submit and run-resume" gap.
Complete a manual or decision step.

Approve or reject a plan that's waiting on human review (issue #187).

Approval re-enqueues the run and the step's flow advances on the
next worker pickup. Rejection re-enqueues with ``approved=false``;
the flow_runner then fails the step with ``feedback`` as the error.

* Runs with ``triggered_by_type='for_each'`` and

Tenant isolation is double-enforced: the route's run-existence

filters by ``tenant_id``.

Elk secret van deze werkruimte, ONTSLEUTELD, als één bestand.

De configuratie-tak draagt een secret als verklaring zonder waarde, want
een tak is iets dat mensen lezen. Een omgeving opzetten of herstellen
vraagt de waarden wél — en twintig ervan overtypen is hoe er een verkeerd
token in productie belandt.

**Alleen een platformbeheerder.** Een werkruimtebeheerder krijgt 403,
ook al mag hij elk van deze waarden los inzien: dit is de enige plek waar
ze allemaal tegelijk in één bestand staan, en dat verdient de hogere
poort. Een servicetoken kan deze poort nooit halen

Geaudit met namen en aantallen, nooit met een waarde — het auditspoor is

Zet de secrets uit dit bestand in deze werkruimte, op NAAM.

Wat het bestand niet noemt blijft zoals het is: een regel zonder waarde

instellingen staan. ``settings: {}`` is wél een uitspraak en maakt ze
leeg. Dezelfde regel als bij de tak — afwezig is niet leeg, en dat is de
regel die een rollback ooit de halve vault kostte.

Alles of niets: een regel die niet klopt weigert het hele bestand. Half
toepassen laat een beheerder achter met een vault waarvan hij niet weet
wat erin staat.
