post.description:
Bulk dismiss — accepts ``ids`` OR ``filter`` (exactly one).

Step one of the operator's two-step clean-up: put rows away without
losing them. Reversible (replay un-dismisses), so the blast radius is
a display change, not data loss — but it is still a change to the
queue, hence an admin or an ``operate``-scoped token, like every other
recovery write here (#744, #976).

Per-row outcomes are tallied, never raised: rows that are already
dismissed or not in a dismissable state come back as ``skipped``.

get.description:
JSON export of filtered rows.

Capped at ``INSPECTOR_MAX_LIMIT`` rows per request — multiple-
page exports are out of scope (issue #332 "Out of scope" —
analytics is a separate epic). Response body is delivered through
a ``StreamingResponse`` so the JSON write happens row-by-row on
the wire rather than via a single ``json.dumps`` of the full
list; with the 100-row cap the difference is cosmetic, but the
shape leaves room to lift the cap later without rewriting the
handler.

post.description:
Permanently delete dismissed rows — administrators only. No undo.

Step two of the clean-up. Only rows that were ALREADY dismissed can
be deleted; the service enforces that and tallies everything else as
``skipped``, so a mis-aimed filter cannot reach live work.

The filter form resolves with ``include_dismissed=True`` regardless
of what the caller passed: the default inspector view HIDES dismissed
rows, so honouring ``includeDismissed: false`` here would resolve to
exactly the set of rows purge is forbidden to touch and always report
zero. Purge only ever operates on the dismissed set by definition.

Release every selected task — same ids-XOR-filter argument as replay.

One selection model drives every operator action on the screen, so the
body shape is deliberately shared rather than cloned.

Bulk replay — accepts ``ids`` OR ``filter`` (exactly one).

Administrators only (epic #744): reads are workspace-wide, writes
are an operator's. The blast radius here is the argument — a filter
form can re-run up to 500 rows in one click.

``filter`` mirrors the GET ``/`` query parameters (state, owner,
workflow, batch, time-range). The route resolves the filter into a
concrete id list (capped at 500 to bound the operation) before
delegating to the service.

Bulk stop — ``ids`` only, never a filter.

The other bulk actions accept a filter because their blast radius is
a display change or a delete of rows the operator already put away.
Stopping ENDS live work, so it stays on the rows somebody actually
selected; a mis-aimed filter here would reach a workspace's whole
queue.

Per-row outcomes are tallied, never raised: rows that had already
finished come back as ``skipped``.

get.description: Single-task detail view — drives the inspector's drawer.

post.description:
Soft-archive a ``failed`` / ``dead_letter`` row — admins only (#744).

Dismissing is the decision that a piece of work will never be done;
that call belongs to the workspace's operator, not to anyone who can
view the queue.

Returns 422 (``ValidationError``) for rows in any other state (live
or successful work is not clean-up); 404 for cross-tenant or missing
rows.

Bring a waiting task's moment forward to now — admins only.

Office hours hold a fan-out's children until the next morning, which
is the point of stating them — and the moment someone needs a way to
overrule it. Releasing does not re-run anything: the state, the
payload and the attempt count are untouched, only the moment moves.

Reset a single task to ``pending`` (idempotent) — admins only.

Epic #744 permission split: every member of the workspace may SEE
the queue, only an administrator may CHANGE it. Replay re-runs work
with real side effects, so it is an operator action.

End a live row — the operator's stop button (#1122).

The action the inspector was missing. Dismiss refuses ``pending`` /
``in_progress`` on purpose: putting a live row away hides it rather
than stopping it. So a row an operator watched re-dispatch itself had
no action at all — "Dismiss all" skipped it in silence, and the only
thing left was to wait out ``max_attempts``.

The row ends terminally at ``failed`` and records who ended it.
Afterwards it is an ordinary finished row: dismissable, then
purgeable.

Same authority as release / replay / dismiss — an administrator, or a
service token the workspace granted ``operate`` (#744, #976): this is
recovery, not administration.

Returns 422 for a row that already reached an end (nothing to stop);
404 for cross-tenant or missing rows.

Execute tool code in the sandbox worker pool.

Validates code via AST analysis, then runs in a pre-warmed worker process.

Gated on WRITE, not admin (#678 B5): an external agent authors a tool
through the MCP connector and must be able to test-run it, otherwise it
ships code it has never seen execute. That is not an escalation — tool
CRUD is already open to any member, so the same principal could always
store this code; running it adds no reach. The code executes in the
sandbox (``SANDBOX-ARCHITECTURE.md``), which holds no tenant data and
reaches no network, and the only tenant row this route touches is loaded
scoped to ``auth.tenant_id``.

Execute a connector REST or GraphQL API call.

Builds an HTTP request from the connector configuration, executes it,
and optionally applies JMESPath response mapping.

If auth_config contains a secretId, resolves the stored secret
before passing to the connector execution service.

Stays ADMIN-only, deliberately, while ``/execute`` opened up (#678 B5).
This route leaves the sandbox: the caller supplies the target URL AND the
auth config, and the backend decrypts a stored tenant secret into that
request. Opening it to a write-scoped token would let a machine credential
point a tenant secret at a host of its choosing — credential exfiltration,
not a test-run. The safe way to give agents connector testing is a route
that executes a STORED connector by id, with the URL and credentials taken
from the tenant's own row rather than from the request body.

Prove a tool's STORED code by running it in the sandbox (#792).

This is the path that satisfies the publish gate. ``/tools/execute``
cannot: it runs caller-supplied functions, which need not be the tool's
stored code, so a stamp there would mean nothing. Here the code comes
from the tool row loaded under ``auth.tenant_id`` and nothing about it is
caller-supplied — only the sample input is.

A clean run stamps ``dry_run_passed_version`` at the tool's current
version; editing the tool afterwards bumps the version and invalidates
the proof. Gated on WRITE for the same reason as ``/tools/execute``: an
external agent authors a tool through the connector and must be able to
prove it, or it can never publish what it built.

Execute a connector ALREADY stored in the caller's tenant (#678 B5).

The safe counterpart to ``/execute-connector``: the caller names which of
its own connectors to run and supplies only the call's inputs, while the
destination and the credentials are read from the tenant's connector row.
Because the body cannot steer where the request goes, a write-scoped
service token can use this — an agent can finally verify the connector it
authored, not just the function tools.

put.description:

Separate from ``PUT /tools/{id}`` for two reasons. First, there
``null`` already means "leave this field alone", so there would be
no way to say "ungroup". Second, grouping is not a change to the
tool's published document — it neither bumps the version nor needs

delete.description:
Remove somebody from the workspace — permanently, and reversibly.

**This does NOT delete a row, and must not be "fixed" into one.** 26
foreign keys across 20 models point at ``users.id`` and most carry no
``ondelete``, so the delete is refused by the database the moment that
person has authored, published or launched anything — and the few that
did succeed would erase authorship the workspace has to keep. The
membership is marked ``removed_at``: it disappears from the roster and
from every owner picker, its sessions are revoked, and the workflow it
wrote three years ago still names its author. An admin adds the same
person again to reinstate them.

A membership in another workspace answers 404, not 403 — a 403 would
confirm the id exists. Suspending signs the person out; re-activating
does not sign them back in. ``role: platform_admin`` — or ``member`` /
``admin`` for somebody who holds that authority — is a platform
administrator's call alone.

post.description:
Mint a password-reset link for a colleague, for the admin to deliver.

The platform cannot send mail until SMTP is configured, which leaves
somebody who has forgotten their password with no way back in. This is the
same single-use, hashed, expiring token the self-service flow mints — only
the delivery is a human errand instead of an inbox, which is why its
window is measured in days.

Refused for a colleague who has been removed, and for a credential that
also has access to another workspace: a password belongs to the
CREDENTIAL, so a link minted here would change the password that person
uses THERE. Those people use the forgotten-password link instead, which
proves possession of the mailbox — or a platform administrator, who
administers every workspace already and so may reset it.

post.description:
Show ONE webhook address to the administrator who asked.

Deliberately the same shape as ``POST /api/v1/secrets/{id}/reveal``, and
for the same reasons: POST because it writes an audit row and because a GET
carrying a credential ends up in proxy logs, browser history and caches
nobody chose; one webhook per call, named in the URL, so there is no
endpoint that hands over every address this workspace has.

The audit row names the webhook and never the address. Writing the
credential into the trail would MOVE the exposure rather than record it —
and the trail is read by more people, and kept far longer, than the screen
that asked.

A refusal writes NOTHING. An audit line for a disclosure that did not
happen makes the trail unreadable as "these are the moments an address left
the building", which is the only question it exists to answer.
Rotate the webhook's secret.  Old token honoured for 24h grace.

get.description: List soft-deleted workflows that can still be restored.

What this deploy can be built from: commands, trigger types, step types,
schedule rules.

Every list is GENERATED from the registry that enforces it — the engine's
mutation registry the ``/{workflow_id}/mutations`` route validates against
(#802 B4), the trigger-type constants, the validator's own authorable-step
set, and ``RULE_KINDS``. So a client reads the vocabulary here instead of
restating it, and no list can advertise something the platform then refuses.
The connector's hand-written guide named nine step types where seven
validate; that is the failure this closes (S1).

``rulesVersion`` is a content hash the client caches on: unchanged hash,
nothing to re-fetch.

Declared BEFORE ``/{workflow_id}`` so the literal ``operations`` segment is
not swallowed by the id path parameter — the same care ``/bulk`` needed in
``publish_approvals.py``. No DB and no tenant data: this describes the
DEPLOY, not a tenant's workflows, so a service token is enough
(``get_auth_context`` admits them).

get.description:
Which workflows name this entity — the answer before you change it.

#845 S5 gave policies, skills and reference docs a reverse view, with the
reasoning that "what breaks if I change this" is the question an author most
needs before editing something shared. The rest of the catalogue never got
one, and a broken tool or agent reference stops a RUN rather than a prompt.

It is not a link-table query, which is why it did not exist: an agent gets
into a workflow by being named in a step's ``contract.owners`` and a tool by
sitting in ``contract.tools.toolIds``, in a plan activity, or on an
automation step's config. Those are keys inside a JSON document — the reason
an author cannot find them by hand either (S8).

``data_table`` (#1234) is the newest kind and the one shared hardest: a
routing table is meant to be used by several processes, and a decision
naming it lives one level deeper still, in
``config.evaluatorArgs.tableId``. Unpublishing it does not break a
reference — it stops the decision routing, silently.

Declared BEFORE ``/{workflow_id}`` so ``using`` is not swallowed by the id
path parameter, the same care ``/operations`` and ``/callable`` needed.

post.description:
Validate a workflow document that is being edited, without saving it.

The SAME answer opening the workflow gives, on the document as it stands
in the editor rather than as it was last saved. One validator, one
catalog, one verdict — whichever way you reach it.

It used to be stateless, and that was the bug. With no catalog every
cross-entity check was skipped, so this route reported only structure:
a decision routing on a table that cannot be read, a step naming a tool
nobody published, an agent whose knowledge will not load — all invisible.
The editor's Validate button calls this route and REPLACES its issue list
with the answer, so pressing it made a real error disappear from the
screen without anything having been fixed. A narrower answer is worse than
no answer when it overwrites a fuller one.

``catalogChecked`` stays in the response: the checks are still skipped when
the repositories behind the catalog are not wired, and a caller has to be
able to see that rather than read silence as health.

get.description: How each judged rule fared across a workflow's runs.

Everything this workflow is made of, in one answer (#1369).

A process is made of agents, flows, tools, tables, knowledge and the
processes it calls. That list existed nowhere: finding it meant opening the
canvas step by step, clicking through to an agent, from there to its tools,
from there to the table behind it — and remembering it yourself.

Two hops, composed. ``find_document_references`` answers the first — which
entities the document NAMES, and in which steps. The second asks the
runtime's own readers what each agent actually receives and what each tool
reaches, because "what is attached" and "what the agent gets" are different
questions with different answers.

Every row carries its SOURCES rather than a bare "used": an entity reached
twice is one dependency with two reasons, and "in these two steps" is what
an author can act on. Whether each one is LIVE is #1370's job.

An unknown id raises ``NotFoundError`` in the service rather than coming
back as an empty list: a workflow that names nothing and a workflow that
does not exist are different answers, and a caller that cannot tell them
apart reports success for a typo.

post.description:
Copy a shared component and point THIS workflow at the copy (#1371).

An agent is shared: editing one from inside a process changes processes the
author never opened. This is the escape hatch — the copy belongs to this
process, every other process stays on the original, and the original is not
modified at all.

Returns the whole document rather than a patch. The repoint rewrites every
site the component was named in, and a caller applying a partial answer
would keep a stale reference on the sites it did not hear about.

get.description:
One page of a workflow's LAUNCHES, newest first (epic #811 S1).

A launch is a run a person or a schedule started. The item results a
FOR EACH produces are runs too, but they belong INSIDE their launch and
never appear here — a launch over 4,415 people is exactly one entry,
carrying ``forEachProgress`` so the row can show "3,180 of 4,415
processed · 12 failed" without a request of its own.

Use ``?archived_only=true`` for archived launches, and ``?status=`` —
repeatable — to narrow to particular run statuses. The status filter is
applied in the QUERY, before the page is cut (epic #811 S2): the
operator's "failed only" view must reach a failure buried under a page
of newer completions, which a client-side filter over the rows already
downloaded could never do.

Paging is keyset: follow ``nextCursor``, never an offset (see
:mod:`src.repositories.paging`).

Cost is flat in page size: one query for the page, one grouped roll-up,
one workflow-name lookup and one batched user-name lookup — not the
per-row pair this endpoint used to do.

get.description:
Which skills are attached to this workflow (S8).

Attaching and detaching both had a route; reading the result back did not.
A link lives OUTSIDE the entity body, so nothing else shows it — which
means nothing distinguished an attach that landed from one that quietly did
nothing. That is the shape of #778, where 27 detach calls all answered
``detached: true`` and not one of those links existed.

What this workflow needs in order to start — per start.

This used to answer ``triggers[0].parameters``: correct for a workflow with
one trigger, and for a workflow with a button AND a schedule an answer about
an arbitrary one, with nothing in the response saying which. It also listed
author-pinned values beside fields to fill in, while a pinned value is
exactly the one a caller must NOT send — ``apply_parameter_defaults``
overwrites it, deliberately, because a field the UI does not show must not
become an injection point (S5).

So every trigger is described, each with its own parameters, each parameter
saying whether the author owns it, and the workflow's constants listed
apart because they belong to no trigger at all.
